:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}- u v\\- u\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u v)&=- v\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- u)&=-1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u v)&=- u\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- v\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}- u\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- v & -1 & 0\\- u & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(-1)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- v)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(- u)\\&=v.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- v)(0)\\&\quad -(-1)(- u)\\&=- u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\v\\- u\end{pmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(u)&=1\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(2 u - e^{v})&=2\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(u)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(2 u - e^{v})&=- e^{v}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\- e^{v}\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\1 & 2 & 0\\0 & - e^{v} & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(2)(1)\\&\quad -(0)(- e^{v})\\&=2.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(1)(1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=-1.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(1)(- e^{v})\\&\quad -(2)(0)\\&=- e^{v}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\- e^{v}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The tangent vectors are

:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\v\end{pmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\cos{(u )})&=- \sin{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\sin{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v)&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\cos{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\sin{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v)&=1\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- \sin{(u )}\\\cos{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- \sin{(u )} & \cos{(u )} & 0\\0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(\cos{(u )})(1)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=\cos{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- \sin{(u )})(1)\\&\quad +(0)(0)\\&=\sin{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- \sin{(u )})(0)\\&\quad -(\cos{(u )})(0)\\&=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem:
Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}v \cos{(u )}\\\sin{(u )}\\- v^{2}\end{pmatrix}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The fundamental vector product is $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$, in that order. Hold the other parameter constant in each partial derivative.

Differentiate the coordinates to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(v \cos{(u )})&=- v \sin{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(\sin{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial u}(- v^{2})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(v \cos{(u )})&=\cos{(u )}\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(\sin{(u )})&=0\\\frac{\partial}{\partial v}(- v^{2})&=- 2 v\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent vectors are

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf r_u&=\begin{pmatrix}- v \sin{(u )}\\\cos{(u )}\\0\end{pmatrix},\\\mathbf r_v&=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{(u )}\\0\\- 2 v\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Form the ordered determinant:

$$
\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\- v \sin{(u )} & \cos{(u )} & 0\\\cos{(u )} & 0 & - 2 v\end{vmatrix}.
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{1}&=(\cos{(u )})(- 2 v)\\&\quad -(0)(0)\\&=- 2 v \cos{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{2}&=-(- v \sin{(u )})(- 2 v)\\&\quad +(0)(\cos{(u )})\\&=- 2 v^{2} \sin{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$


$$
\begin{aligned}(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)_{3}&=(- v \sin{(u )})(0)\\&\quad -(\cos{(u )})(\cos{(u )})\\&=- \cos^{2}{(u )}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}- 2 v \cos{(u )}\\- 2 v^{2} \sin{(u )}\\- \cos^{2}{(u )}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac12x^2+y^2,$ find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta,$ where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(r, \theta)=r \cos 3\theta,$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial r}\cos\theta - \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta}\sin\theta
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-3r\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=z^3(x^2+2y^2),$ find $\dfrac{\partial w}{\partial \theta},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=2x{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=4y{z}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r, \theta,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(2r{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(4r{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{z}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{∂w}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂w}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2xy+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2x+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\left(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\left(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2yz,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+2z\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2z)r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy+{y}^{2}z+x{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y,z)$ with three independent variables $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ and $z=z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+2xz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2rz\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂y}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{r}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & ={r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\left(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\right)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)={y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂g}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂\theta } & =0\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂w}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=x,\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =0\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=2r+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=2,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2r}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $g(r,\theta )={r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$

$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{∂f}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r}=\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ,\,\frac{∂f}{∂\theta }=2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \end{aligned}

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(r,\theta )=r\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂y},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $u(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xyz,$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z}=2{x}^{2}z+xy\end{aligned}

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}(2z{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ).\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that $v(x,y,z)=2y-xz,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

$$

:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4{x}^{2}{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta )=r(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ),$ find $\frac{∂u}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)={x}^{3}{z}^{4}+{y}^{3}{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $p(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂p}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $v(r,\theta )={r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ find $\frac{∂v}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$
\frac{∂v}{∂x}=\frac{∂v}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $v$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂r}=2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{∂v}{∂\theta }=-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂v}{∂x} & =(2r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂z}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r,\theta ,$ and $z,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =2{r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}z\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta )=r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1),$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂x},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1,\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta }=-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{r}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y,z)=x{z}^{4}+y,$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂z}\cdot \frac{∂z}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}={z}^{4},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={z}^{4}, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =({z}^{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={z}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+y,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z+{z}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂z},$ where $(x,y,z)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the corresponding cylindrical polar coordinates.

:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta)=- 3 r^{3} (\sin {2 \theta} - 3)$, find $\frac{∂u}{∂x}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂x}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}\sin \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=- 9 r^{2} (\sin {2 \theta} - 3),\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}=- 6 r^{3} \cos {2 \theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =(- 9 r^{2} (\sin {2 \theta} - 3))\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}(- 6 r^{3} \cos {2 \theta})\sin \theta \\ & =27{r}^{2}\cos \theta-9{r}^{2}\sin 2\theta\cos \theta+6{r}^{2}\cos 2\theta\sin \theta \\ & =-3{r}^{2}(-9\cos \theta+3\sin 2\theta\cos \theta-2\cos 2\theta\sin \theta).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $u(r,\theta)=- 4 r^{2}$, find $\frac{∂u}{∂y}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂u}{∂y}=\frac{∂u}{∂r}\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}\cos \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $u$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂r}=- 8 r,\,\frac{∂u}{∂\theta}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =(- 8 r)\sin \theta+\frac{1}{r}(0)\cos \theta \\ & =- 8 r \sin {\theta}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $h(r,\theta)=- 3 r^{2} (\cos {4 \theta} - 1)$, find $\frac{∂h}{∂x}$, where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta)$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
:question/worked-solution:
We will make use of the following chain rule formula:

$$
\frac{∂h}{∂x}=\frac{∂h}{∂r}\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}\frac{∂h}{∂\theta}\sin \theta.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $r$ and $\theta:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r}=- 6 r (\cos {4 \theta} - 1),\,\frac{∂h}{∂\theta}=12 r^{2} \sin {4 \theta}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =(- 6 r (\cos {4 \theta} - 1))\cos \theta-\frac{1}{r}(12 r^{2} \sin {4 \theta})\sin \theta \\ & =6r\cos \theta-6r\cos 4\theta\cos \theta-12r\sin 4\theta\sin \theta \\ & =-3r(-2\cos \theta+2\cos 4\theta\cos \theta+4\sin 4\theta\sin \theta).\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Differentiate $x\cos x.$
:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=\cos x .$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	 (x\cos x)' &=   u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\\
						&= (x)'\cdot \cos x + x\cdot (\cos x)'\\
					   & = 1 \cdot \cos x + x (-\sin x)\\
					  & =  \cos x - x \sin x					

\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=x^2\ln x,$ find $f'(x).$
:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = x^2$ and $v(x)=\ln x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2})}^{′}ln⁡x+{x}^{2}{(ln⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =2x\cdot ln⁡x+{x}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \\  & =2xln⁡x+x \\  & =x(2ln⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=e^x\sin x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\dfrac \pi 2.$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^x$ and $v(x)=\sin{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = e^x,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+sin⁡x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\dfrac\pi 2$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi /2} & ={e}^{\pi /2}(cos⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+sin⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e^{\pi/2}.$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x) = x^{-3}\log_{2} x$, find $f^{′}(x)$.

4.

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y = 8x^{3}\sin x$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x = \frac{π}{2}$.

:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=3{x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=3{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{tan}x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(3{x}^{2})({sec}^{2}x)+(\operatorname{tan}x)(6x) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}x+6x\operatorname{tan}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=\pi } & =3{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}x+6x\operatorname{tan}x{|}_{x=\pi } \\  & =3(\pi )^{2}{sec}^{2}(\pi )+6(\pi )\operatorname{tan}(\pi ) \\  & =3{\pi }^{2}\cdot 1+6\pi \cdot 0 \\  & =3{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $3{\pi }^{2}.$

:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(x-1)\operatorname{ln}(2x+1),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x-1$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}(2x+1).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{2x+1}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x-1)\cdot \frac{2}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1)\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2(x-1)}{2x+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & =\frac{2(0-1)}{2(0)+1}+\operatorname{ln}(2(0)+1) \\  & =(-2)+\operatorname{ln}(1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-2.$

:question/problem:
If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is defined by the equation $y=f(x)\cdot h(x),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$

Slope $\,=${{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

:question/problem:
If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is defined by the equation $y=f(x)\cdot h(x),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$

Slope $\,=${{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Recall that $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}$ and $h(x)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x})=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}x}+h\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{x}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{x} \\  & =-2{e}^{x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & =-2{e}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =-2{e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =2{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2{e}^{\pi }.$

:question/problem: Differentiate ${e}^{x}cos⁡x.$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=x\cdot {3}^{x},$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(x)^{′}\cdot {3}^{x}+x\cdot ({3}^{x})^{′} \\  & ={3}^{x}+(x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{x}) \\  & ={3}^{x}+x\operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{x} \\  & =(1+x\operatorname{ln}⁡3){3}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x)={x}^{2}{e}^{x},$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$

:question/problem: Differentiate ${e}^{x}tan⁡x.$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=cos⁡xlog⁡x,$ find ${f}^{′}(x).$
:question/worked-solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=cos⁡x$ and $v(x)=log⁡x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(cos⁡x)}^{′}log⁡x+cos⁡x{(log⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =(-sin⁡x)(log⁡x)+(cos⁡x)\left(\frac{1}{xln⁡10}\right) \\  & =\frac{cos⁡x}{xln⁡10}-sin⁡xlog⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)={e}^{x}$ and $v(x)=2+sin⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}({e}^{x}sec⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =({e}^{x})^{′}\cdot (2+sin⁡(x))+{e}^{x}\cdot (2+sin⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =({e}^{x})(2+sin⁡(x))+({e}^{x})(cos⁡(x)) \\  & =(2+sin⁡(x)){e}^{x}+{e}^{x}cos⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=2{x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=cos⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}^{2}cos⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(2{x}^{2})^{′}\cdot cos⁡(x)+2{x}^{2}\cdot (cos⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =(4x)(cos⁡(x))+(2{x}^{2})(-sin⁡(x)) \\  & =4xcos⁡(x)-2{x}^{2}sin⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $v(x)=tan⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{x}tan⁡(x))^{′} & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(\sqrt{x})^{′}\cdot tan⁡(x)+\sqrt{x}\cdot (tan⁡(x))^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}(tan⁡(x))+(\sqrt{x})({sec}^{2}⁡(x)) \\  & =\frac{tan⁡(x)}{2\sqrt{x}}+\sqrt{x}{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)={4}^{x}$ and $v(x)=tan⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({4}^{x})}^{′}tan⁡(x)+{4}^{x}{(tan⁡(x))}^{′} \\  & =({4}^{x}ln⁡(4))tan⁡(x)+{4}^{x}({sec}^{2}⁡(x)) \\  & ={4}^{x}ln⁡(4)tan⁡(x)+{4}^{x}{sec}^{2}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=(x+2)cos⁡x,$ then the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x+2$ and $v(x)=cos⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-sin⁡x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x+2)\cdot (-sin⁡x)+cos⁡x\cdot 1 \\  & =-(x+2)sin⁡x+cos⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\frac{\pi }{2}} & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)sin⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+cos⁡\frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =-(\frac{\pi }{2}+2)(1)+0 \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-\frac{\pi }{2}-2.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=(x-1)ln⁡(4x-3),$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x-1$ and $v(x)=ln⁡(4x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{4}{4x-3}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(x-1)\cdot \frac{4}{4x-3}+ln⁡(4x-3).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=1$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =(1-1)\cdot \frac{4}{4(1)-3}+ln⁡(4(1)-3) \\  & =0+ln⁡(1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $0.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=({x}^{2}-4x+7){e}^{x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$ is{{field-1}}.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{2}-4x+7$ and $v(x)={e}^{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x-4,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =({x}^{2}-4x+7)\cdot {e}^{x}+{e}^{x}\cdot (2x-4) \\  & ={e}^{x}({x}^{2}-2x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=0} & ={{e}^{x}({x}^{2}-2x+3)|}_{x=0} \\  & =1\cdot (0-0+3)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $3.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=(3x-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=3x-2$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(3x-2)\cdot \frac{1}{x}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{3x-2}{x}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=1$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{3x-2}{x}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{3(1)-2}{1}+3\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $1.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y={e}^{x}sin⁡x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi .$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)={e}^{x}$ and $v(x)=sin⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=cos⁡x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+(sin⁡x)\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi $ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi } & ={{e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x)|}_{x=\pi } \\  & ={e}^{\pi }(-1+0) \\  & =-{e}^{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-{e}^{\pi }.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=({x}^{3}-1){e}^{x},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)={x}^{3}-1$ and $v(x)={e}^{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =({x}^{3}-1)\cdot {e}^{x}+{e}^{x}\cdot (3{x}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{x}({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=2$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={{e}^{x}({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-1)|}_{x=2} \\  & ={e}^{2}({2}^{3}+3(2)^{2}-1) \\  & =19{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $19{e}^{2}.$

:question/problem: If a curve $\mathcal{C}$ is given by $y=x\operatorname{ln}⁡x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=e.$
:question/worked-solution:

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =x\cdot \frac{1}{x}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot 1 \\  & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=e} & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡e \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $2.$

:question/problem:
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(3 x^{2} + x - 1)\cdot (\ln{\left(x \right)})$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=e^{2}$.

Slope $=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=3 x^{2} + x - 1$ and $v(x)=\ln{\left(x \right)}.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=6 x + 1,\quad v'(x)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(3 x^{2} + x - 1)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+(\ln{\left(x \right)})\cdot (6 x + 1) \\ &=\frac{6 x^{2} \ln{\left(x \right)} + 3 x^{2} + x \ln{\left(x \right)} + x - 1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e^{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=e^{2}} &=(3 (e^{2})^{2} + (e^{2}) - 1)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{(e^{2})}\right)+(\ln{\left((e^{2}) \right)})\cdot (6 (e^{2}) + 1) \\ &=(-1 + e^{2} + 3 e^{4})\cdot (e^{-2})+(2)\cdot (1 + 6 e^{2}) \\ &=- \frac{1}{e^{2}} + 3 + 15 e^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $- \frac{1}{e^{2}} + 3 + 15 e^{2}.$

:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(4 e^{x})\cdot (x + 1)$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=4 e^{x}$ and $v(x)=x + 1.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=4 e^{x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(4 e^{x})\cdot (1)+(x + 1)\cdot (4 e^{x}) \\ &=4 \left(x + 2\right) e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=0} &=(4 e^{(0)})\cdot (1)+((0) + 1)\cdot (4 e^{(0)}) \\ &=(4)\cdot (1)+(1)\cdot (4) \\ &=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $8.$

:question/problem:
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(- x^{2} - x - 1)\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)})$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$.

Slope $=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=- x^{2} - x - 1$ and $v(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=- 2 x - 1,\quad v'(x)=\cos{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(- x^{2} - x - 1)\cdot (\cos{\left(x \right)})+(\sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (- 2 x - 1) \\ &=- x^{2} \cos{\left(x \right)} - 2 x \sin{\left(x \right)} - x \cos{\left(x \right)} - \sin{\left(x \right)} - \cos{\left(x \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=\frac{\pi}{4}} &=(- \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2} - \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - 1)\cdot (\cos{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \right)})+(\sin{\left(\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \right)})\cdot (- 2 \left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - 1) \\ &=(-1 - \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi^{2}}{16})\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\cdot (- \frac{\pi}{2} - 1) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{2} \left(- 12 \pi - 32 - \pi^{2}\right)}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $\frac{\sqrt{2} \left(- 12 \pi - 32 - \pi^{2}\right)}{32}.$

:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(- e^{x})\cdot (x + 3)$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$.
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=- e^{x}$ and $v(x)=x + 3.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=- e^{x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(- e^{x})\cdot (1)+(x + 3)\cdot (- e^{x}) \\ &=- \left(x + 4\right) e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=0} &=(- e^{(0)})\cdot (1)+((0) + 3)\cdot (- e^{(0)}) \\ &=(-1)\cdot (1)+(3)\cdot (-1) \\ &=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $-4.$

$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(2x+1)\cdot \frac{1}{x}+(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=2^{x}$ and $v(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}(u(x)v(x))' &=u'(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v'(x) \\ &=(2^{x})'\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(2^{x})\cdot (\sin{\left(x \right)})' \\ &=(2^{x} \ln{\left(2 \right)})(\sin{\left(x \right)}) \\ &\quad +(2^{x})(\cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &=2^{x} \ln{\left(2 \right)} \sin{\left(x \right)} \\ &\quad +(2^{x} \cos{\left(x \right)})\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem: Given that $f(x) = 6\log_{5} x\ln x$, find $f^{′}(x)$.

Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)=6\log_{5} x$ and $v(x)=\ln x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & =(6\log_{5} x)^{′}\ln x+6\log_{5} x(\ln x)^{′} \\  & =(\frac{6}{x \ln{\left(5 \right)}})(\ln x)+(6\log_{5} x)(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{6\log_{5} x}{x} + \frac{6\ln x}{x\ln 5}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=4 \\ x+2y &=16\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x+2y &=16 \\
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\\
	4+3y &=16\\
	3y &=12\\
	y &=4
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	x &= 4 + y \\
	   &= 4 + (4) \\
	   &=8
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2u+9v-6 &=0 \\ 2u+6v-8 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:


$$\qquad\:\:\:
\begin{cases}{\color{red}2u+9v-6=0}\hspace{2em}{\color{red}(1)} \\ {\color{blue}2u+6v-8=0}\hspace{2em}{\color{blue}(2)}\end{cases}.$$



We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \\
2u+6v &= 8 \\
2u &= 8 - 6v \\
u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \\
u &= 4 - 3v
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \\
2+3v &= 0 \\
3v &= -2 \\
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \\
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \\
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \\
	2u-12 &= 0 \\
	2u &= 12 \\
	u &= 6
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

:question/problem:
Using the method of substitution, find the solution of
$$
\displaystyle \left\{\begin{aligned}-3p + q &=-9 \\ 5p + 4q &=32\end{aligned}\right.
$$.
:question/worked-solution: The first equation gives $q=3p-9$. Substitute into the second equation: $$5p+4(3p-9)=32\implies17p=68\implies p=4.$$ Hence $q=3(4)-9=3$. Substitution into both original equations gives $-9$ and $32$, as required.

$$

:question/problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $p-q?$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3p &=15 \\ p+2q &=9.\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $p$ by dividing both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =15 \\ p & =5\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $p=5$ into $p+2q=9,$ then we can find the value of $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$

:question/problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $y-x?$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y &=0 \\ 5y-15x+10 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}21x-9y &=0 && \,\,(1) \\ 5y-15x+10 &=0 && \,\,(2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can isolate $y$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5y-15x+10 & =0 \\ 5y & =15x-10 \\ y & =3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $3x-2$  into equation $(1)$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}21x-9y & =0 \\ 21x-9(3x-2) & =0 \\ 21x-27x+18 & =0 \\ -6x+18 & =0 \\ 18 & =6x \\ 3 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $x=3$ into $y=3x-2,$ then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3x-2 \\ y & =3(3)-2 \\ y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=3,\,y=7.$ So,

$$
y-x=7-3=4.
$$

:question/problem:
The pastry shop's total cost and revenue per month (in dollars) from selling cakes can be modeled by the equations $y=1\,600+5n$ and $y=64+17n,$ respectively, where $n$ is the number of cakes sold. 

Solve the system below using the substitution method to find the exact number of cakes needed to break even and the revenue made.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1\,600+5n \\ y &=64+17n\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The pastry shop breaks even when$\,$
{{field-1}}
$\,$cakes are produced. 

The revenue made when selling this number of cakes is$\,$
{{field-2}}
$\,$dollars.
:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that $y$ is isolated in the first equation. Therefore, we can replace $y$ with $1\,600+5n$ in the second equation and solve for $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =64+17n \\ 1\,600+5n & =64+17n \\ 1\,600+5n-64 & =64+17n-64 \\ 1\,536+5n & =17n \\ 1\,536+5n-5n & =17n-5n \\ 1\,536 & =12n \\ \frac{1\,536}{12} & =\frac{12n}{12} \\ 128 & =n \\ n & =128\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $n=128$ into $y=64+17n$, then we can find the value of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=64+17(128)=2\,240\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solution to the system of equations is $n=128$ and $y=2\,240.$
Therefore, the pastry shop breaks even when $128$ units are produced, and the revenue made when selling this number of units is $2\,240$ dollars.

:question/problem:
Mary wonders where and when they'd meet if Sam left home $3.8$ minutes earlier and walked with a speed of $50$ meters per minute. She finds that the distance $d$ from home they'd meet can be modeled using the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}d+60t &=960 \\ d-50t &=190.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $t$ is the time (in minutes) since Mary left the community park.

Mary and Sam would meet$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$minutes after Mary left the community park.

Mary and Sam would meet at a distance of $\,$
{{field-2}}$\,$meters from home.
:question/worked-solution:
To solve the given system of linear equations, we will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the second equation looks like the easiest.

Using the second equation, we can isolate $d$ adding to both sides of the equation $50t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d-50t &=190 \\ d &=190+50t\end{aligned}
$$

So, we replace $d$ with $190+50t$ in the first equation and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d+60t=960 \\ (190+50t)+60t & =960 \\ 190+110t & =960 \\ 110t & =960-190 \\ 110t & =770 \\ t & =\frac{770}{110} \\ t & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, they would have met after $t=7$ minutes.

If we substitute $t=7$ into $d=190+50t$, we can find the value of $d:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =190+50t \\  & =190+50(7) \\  & =540\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, they meet at a distance of $540$ meters from home.

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x - 8y - 31 &=0 \\ 2x - 4y - 6 &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x - 8y - 31 &=0 && (1) \\ 2x - 4y - 6 &=0 && (2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 2x - 4y - 6 &= 0 \\ 2x - 4y &= 6 \\ 2x &= 6 + 4y \\ x &= \dfrac{6 + 4y}{2} \\ x &= 3 + 2y \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=3+2y$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6(3 + 2y) - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 18 + 12y - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ -13 + 4y &= 0 \\ 4y &= 13 \\ y &= \dfrac{13}{4} \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $x$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 6x - 8y - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 8\left(\dfrac{13}{4}\right) - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 26 - 31 &= 0 \\ 6x - 57 &= 0 \\ 6x &= 57 \\ x &= \dfrac{19}{2} \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=\dfrac{19}{2}$ and

$$
y=\dfrac{13}{4}
$$

, which can be written as

$$
\left(\dfrac{19}{2},\dfrac{13}{4}\right)
$$

:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
:question/worked-solution:
Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}7a - 8b + 41 &=0 && (1) \\ 4a - 4b + 20 &=0 && (2)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $a$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} 4a - 4b + 20 &= 0 \\ 4a - 4b &= -20 \\ 4a &= -20 + 4b \\ a &= \dfrac{-20 + 4b}{4} \\ a &= -5 + b \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $a=-5+b$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $b$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 7a - 8b + 41 &= 0 \\ 7(-5 + b) - 8b + 41 &= 0 \\ -35 + 7b - 8b + 41 &= 0 \\ 6 - b &= 0 \\ -b &= -6 \\ b &= 6 \end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute

$$
b=6
$$

into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $a$:

$$
\begin{aligned} 7a - 8b + 41 &= 0 \\ 7a - 8\left(6\right) + 41 &= 0 \\ 7a - 48 + 41 &= 0 \\ 7a - 7 &= 0 \\ 7a &= 7 \\ a &= 1 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=1$ and

$$
b=6
$$

, which can be written as

$$
\left(1,6\right)
$$

Using the method of substitution, find the solution of

Using the second equation, we can isolate $d$ adding to both sides of the equation $50t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d-50t &=190 \\ d &=190+50t\end{aligned}
$$

So, we replace $d$ with $190+50t$ in the first equation and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}d+60t=960 \\ (190+50t)+60t & =960 \\ 190+110t & =960 \\ 110t & =960-190 \\ 110t & =770 \\ t & =\frac{770}{110} \\ t & =7.\end{aligned}

$$

Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d s,
$$ where $C$ is the arc of a semicircle of radius $4$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, as shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In this case, $C$ is a semicircle of radius $r = 4.$ Its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L=\pi r=4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = 4\pi.
$$

:question/problem:
![](images/84/84de7754ed9244e3d646e452f6ed6dab349c130d17eae1d4dbc94cb52bd761e1.png)

Calculate $$
\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d s,
$$ where $C$ is the path shown above, traversed once counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The path $C$ is made up of three parts, as shown below:

![](images/f4/f4e80a23910612bd55e7578a074f23c76535139889faff479c4dd0521e7496ff.png)

Now, we make use of the following facts:

- If $C = C_1 \cup C_2 \cup C_3$ is a piecewise-smooth curve, we have

$$
\int_{C}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s =  \int_{C_1}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s + \int_{C_2}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s + \int_{C_3}f(x,y)\,\textrm d s.
$$

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

The path $C_1$ is a semicircle of radius $r = 3.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\int_{C_1} \,\textrm ds = \dfrac{1}{2}(2 \pi r) = 3\pi.
$$

The paths $C_2$ and $C_3$ are hypotenuses of right triangles whose legs have lengths $3$ and $4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\int_{C_2} \,\textrm ds = \int_{C_3} \,\textrm ds = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = 3\pi + 5 + 5 = 3\pi + 10.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the curves $C_1$ and $C_2,$ defined parametrically as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\hspace{1em}{\mathbf{r}}_{1}(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{9}{t}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}t⟩, & 0\le t\le 3 \\ {C}_{2}:\hspace{1em}{\mathbf{r}}_{2}(u) & =⟨3{u}^{3},\hspace{0.222em}3u⟩, & 0\le u\le 1\end{aligned}
$$

Now suppose $$
\displaystyle\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = k
$$ for some function $f(x,y)$ and real number $k.$ Which of the following must be true?

- $$
\displaystyle\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = 3k
$$

- $$
\displaystyle\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = k
$$

- $$
\displaystyle\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = k
$$
:question/worked-solution:
Line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parametrization and orientation.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement. 

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. Notice that $C_1$ and $C_2$ are different parameterizations of the same curve. Since line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parameterization, we have

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = k.
$$

 
To see that $C_1$ and $C_2$ represent the same curve, we can convert each parametrization to Cartesian form. In doing so, we find that both parameterizations give the Cartesian curve

$$
x = \dfrac{1}{9}y^3, \quad 0\leq y\leq 3.
$$

- Statement III is true. Reversing the curve's orientation does *not* change the value of a line integral with respect to arc length. Therefore, we have

$$
\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds  = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm ds = k.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:question/problem:

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.

$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is a line segment of length $4.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=4.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=2\pi +4=2(\pi +2).

:question/worked-solution:
Line integrals with respect to arc length are independent of the choice of parametrization and orientation.

$$

$$

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=4.

Now, we make use of the following facts:

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s.

- The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $r=\frac{34}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}\,\text{d}s=\frac{1}{4}(2\pi r)=\frac{17 \pi}{3} .
$$

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle where both legs have a length of $\frac{34}{3}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}\,\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\frac{34}{3}}^{2}+{\frac{34}{3}}^{2}}=\frac{34 \sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=\frac{17 \pi}{3}+\frac{34 \sqrt{2}}{3}=\frac{17}{3}(\pi+2\sqrt{2}).
$$

:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length equals the length $L$ of the path:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
L=\frac{1}{2}(2\pi r)=3\pi.
$$

$$
\int_C \,\mathrm{d}s=3\pi.
$$

The diameter is not traversed. Reversing direction would leave the arc length unchanged.

:question/worked-solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length equals the length $L$ of the path:

$$
\int_C \,\mathrm{d}s=L.

First find the diameter using the endpoint coordinates. The right triangle below is an auxiliary construction, not an additional path:

![Right triangle with horizontal and vertical legs of length 4 along diameter AB](images/df/df4ccec99dcb2e5bc87533203c10475d5052c1dbc46ee699c4ce5f7d3695e7fb.png)

The coordinate differences are $2-(-2)=4$ and $3-(-1)=4$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
d=AB&=\sqrt{(2-(-2))^2+(3-(-1))^2}\\
&=\sqrt{4^2+4^2}=4\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

A full traversal has length equal to the circumference:

$$
L=\pi d=4\pi\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\oint_C \,\mathrm{d}s=4\pi\sqrt{2}.
$$

A closed path has zero net displacement, but its arc length is positive. Clockwise traversal does not make an integral with respect to $s$ negative.

:question/problem:
Consider the curves

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_1:\quad \mathbf r_1(t)&=\langle t,t^2\rangle, &0\le t\le 2,\\
C_2:\quad \mathbf r_2(u)&=\langle 2u,4u^2\rangle, &0\le u\le 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose $f$ is continuous along the curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3.
$$

The notation $-C_1$ means $C_1$ with its orientation reversed. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
For $C_1$, eliminating $t$ gives $y=x^2$ with $0\le x\le 2$. For $C_2$, $x=2u$ gives $y=4u^2=x^2$, again with $0\le x\le 2$. Both trace this entire parabolic arc once, in the same direction; equivalently, $\mathbf r_2(u)=\mathbf r_1(2u)$.

Independence of parametrization gives

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3.
$$

Changing parameter speed does not multiply this value by $2$, so the proposed value $-6$ is incorrect. Independence of orientation also gives

$$
\int_{-C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3,
$$

so the proposed value $3$ is incorrect. Select only the statement with $\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=-3$. A scalar line integral may be negative when $f$ takes negative values; the nonnegative arc-length element does not force the integral to be positive.

:question/problem:
The diagram shows a curve $C$ from $A$ to $B$ and the same curve $-C$ traversed from $B$ to $A$. Each path traverses the curve once.

![The same curve with opposite orientations: C from A to B and -C from B to A.](images/e4/e4f68e10429fa4bda69366751c303216d27df995edf2502b61ab9bfe84c3ff45.png)

Suppose $f$ is continuous along the curve and

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=6.
$$

What is the value of $\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
:question/worked-solution:
A scalar line integral with respect to arc length is independent of orientation. Reversing the arrows does not change the arc-length element $\mathrm{d}s$ or the values of $f$ along the curve. Therefore,

$$
\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=6.
$$

The answer is $6$. Reversing orientation does not negate the integral, cancel it, or count the curve twice.

:question/problem:
The curve $C_1$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_1(t)=\langle\sqrt{1+9t^2},3t\rangle
$$

for $0\le t\le \frac13$. The curve $C_2$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\langle\sqrt{1+(1-2u)^2},1-2u\rangle
$$

for $0\le u\le \frac12$.

Suppose $f$ is continuous along the curves and

$$
\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

The notation $-C_2$ means $C_2$ with its orientation reversed. Which statements must be true for every such $f$? Select all that apply.
:question/worked-solution:
For $C_1$, $y=3t$, so $x=\sqrt{1+y^2}$ and $y$ increases from $0$ to $1$. For $C_2$, $y=1-2u$, so $x=\sqrt{1+y^2}$ and $y$ decreases from $1$ to $0$. Thus both trace exactly once the same branch and interval,

$$
x=\sqrt{1+y^2},\qquad 0\le y\le 1,
$$

with opposite orientations. In particular,

$$
\mathbf r_2(u)=\mathbf r_1\!\left(\frac{1-2u}{3}\right).
$$

A scalar line integral with respect to arc length is independent of both parametrization and orientation. Hence

$$
\int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

Reversing $C_2$ once more also preserves the value:

$$
\int_{-C_2} f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=k.
$$

The parameter change has derivative $-2/3$, but this is not a factor multiplying the line integral: the speed factor in $\mathrm{d}s$ and the parameter interval change together. The proposed value $2k/3$ is therefore not guaranteed. It agrees with $k$ when $k=0$, but fails, for example, when $f=1$ and $k$ is the positive length of this arc.

Select the statements with values $k$ on $C_2$ and on $-C_2$.
