The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy})\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}\,j\text{ }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{3}$ and $y=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{{t}^{3}}}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{t}{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{t}{2}\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2t}+\frac{t}{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}t+\frac{1}{2}t \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=3t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨2,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{5}{1+25(1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25} \\  & =\frac{5}{26}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\frac{1}{t},t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z))⟩ \\  & =⟨-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=\frac{1}{t},$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\cdot ⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩ \\  & =(-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 2t+(-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))] & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{y}+z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨4,\operatorname{ln}t,{e}^{t}⟩$ at the point $t=2.$

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+z)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y},x{e}^{y},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=4,$ $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},4{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t},1⟩ \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =t\cdot 0+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =4+{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=2$ is

$$

:question/problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+{e}^{t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))].$

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,k \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,i-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,j+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k)\cdot (i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t-2t\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={t}^{2}+1$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j)\cdot (2t\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\cdot 2t+1\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$

:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=x^{2} - y^{2}$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨- 3 t + 1,- t - 1⟩$ at the point $t=-2.$
:question/worked-solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x^{2} - y^{2}),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x^{2} - y^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2 x,- 2 y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=- 3 t + 1$, $y=- t - 1$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2 \left(- 3 t + 1\right),- 2 \left(- t - 1\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 6 t + 2,2 t + 2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 3 t + 1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t - 1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨- 6 t + 2,2 t + 2⟩\cdot ⟨-3,-1⟩ \\  & =\left(- 6 t + 2\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)+\left(2 t + 2\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\  & =16 t - 8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=-2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-2))] & =16 (-2) - 8 \\  & =-40.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$

Next, we substitute $x=t - 2$, $y=3 t + 2$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨- 6 \left(t - 2\right),- 4 \left(3 t + 2\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨- 6 t + 12,- 12 t - 8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t - 2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t + 2)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\mathbf{a}=\langle 1,-4,2 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b}=\langle 0,-2,1 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c}=\langle -1,0,3 \rangle.$
:question/worked-solution:
The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by three vectors is given by the absolute value of their triple product.

First, we compute the triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{vmatrix}-(-4)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2\cdot 3-1\cdot 0)+4(0\cdot 3-1\cdot (-1))+2(0\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =-6+4-4 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the absolute value. So the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped is

$$
V = |-6| = 6.
$$

:question/problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{a}=\langle k,2,1 \rangle,$ $\mathbf{b}=\langle -2,-1,1 \rangle,$ and $\mathbf{c}=\langle -1,1,2 \rangle$ are coplanar.
:question/worked-solution:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =\begin{vmatrix}k & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =k\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =k(-1\cdot 2-1\cdot 1)-2(-2\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1)+(-2\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-3k+6-3 \\  & =-3k+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}\cdot (\mathbf{b}\times \mathbf{c}) & =0 \\ -3k+3 & =0 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=1$.

:question/problem: Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB},$ $\overrightarrow{AC},$ and $\overrightarrow{AD},$ given the points $A(3,-1,2),$ $B(2,1,1),$ $C(-1,2,1),$ and $D(4,4,2).$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overrightarrow{AB},$ $\overrightarrow{AC},$ and $\overrightarrow{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-1,2,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =\mathbf{c}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(-\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =-4\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k} \\  & =⟨-4,3,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =\mathbf{d}-\mathbf{a} \\  & =(4\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k})-(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}) \\  & =\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j} \\  & =⟨1,5,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}+(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-4 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(3\cdot 0-5\cdot (-1))-2((-4)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-1))-((-4)\cdot 5-1\cdot 3) \\  & =-5-2+23 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB},$ $\overrightarrow{AC},$ and $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is

$$

$$

$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by three vectors is given by the absolute value of their triple product.

First, we compute the triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 5 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-4 & 2 \\ 5 & 1\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}+5\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 5\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-((-4)\cdot 1-5\cdot 2)-2(1\cdot 1-0\cdot 2)+5(1\cdot 5-0\cdot (-4)) \\  & =14-2+25 \\  & =37\end{aligned}
$$

    

Finally, we take the absolute value. So the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped is

$$
V=|37|=37.
$$

:question/problem: Find $t$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{p}=⟨9,9,-2⟩,$ $\mathbf{q}=⟨5,6,0⟩,$ and $\mathbf{r}=⟨4,t,t⟩$ are coplanar.

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =\begin{vmatrix}9 & 9 & -2 \\ 5 & 6 & 0 \\ 4 & t & t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}6 & 0 \\ t & t\end{vmatrix}-9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 4 & t\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 4 & t\end{vmatrix} \\  & =9(6\cdot t-t\cdot 0)-9(5\cdot t-4\cdot 0)-2(5\cdot t-4\cdot 6) \\  & =54t-45t-10t+48 \\  & =48-t.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$

$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $t=48.$

$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =3(0\cdot 3-(-2)\cdot (-3))+(2\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-3))-2(2\cdot (-2)-(-1)\cdot 0) \\  & =-18+3+8 \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find $x$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{a}=⟨12,-2x,1⟩$ , $\mathbf{b}=⟨1,5,-2⟩$ and $\mathbf{c}=⟨-9,4,8⟩$  are coplanar.

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =\begin{vmatrix}12 & -2x & 1 \\ 1 & 5 & -2 \\ -9 & 4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =12\cdot \begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ 4 & 8\end{vmatrix}-(-2x)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -9 & 8\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 5 \\ -9 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =12(5\cdot 8-4\cdot (-2))+2x(1\cdot 8-(-9)\cdot (-2))+(1\cdot 4-5\cdot (-9)) \\  & =576-20x+49 \\  & =625-20x.\end{aligned}

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 625-20x & =0 \\ 20x & =625 \\ x & =\frac{125}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{a}=⟨-1,1,1⟩$, $\mathbf{b}=⟨2,1,0⟩$, and $\mathbf{c}=⟨k,-2,-3⟩$ are coplanar.

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ k & -2 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -3\end{vmatrix}-1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ k & -3\end{vmatrix}+\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ k & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-(1\cdot (-3)-(-2)\cdot 0)-(2\cdot (-3)-k\cdot 0)+(2\cdot (-2)-k\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6-4-k \\  & =5-k.\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨0,2,2⟩$, $b=⟨-1,3,-1⟩$, and $c=⟨k,0,1⟩$ are coplanar.

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot(b\times c)&=\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ k & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\\ &=((0)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix})+((-2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ k & 1\end{vmatrix})+((2)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ k & 0\end{vmatrix})\\ &=((0)\cdot ((3)\cdot (1)-(-1)\cdot (0)))+((-2)\cdot ((-1)\cdot (1)-(-1)\cdot (k)))+((2)\cdot ((-1)\cdot (0)-(3)\cdot (k)))\\ &=((0)\cdot (3))+((-2)\cdot (k-1))+((2)\cdot (-3k))\\ &=(0)+(2-2k)+(-6k)\\ &=2-8k\end{aligned}

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-8k&=0\\ -8k&=-2\\ k&=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=\frac{1}{4}.$

$$

V=|(2\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times3\mathbf{a})|.
$$

Factor out the two scale factors. A cyclic change from $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}$ to $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a}$ preserves the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2\mathbf{b})\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times3\mathbf{a})
&=6\,\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a})\\
&=6\,\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\\
&=6(-5)=-30.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, take the absolute value:

$$
V=|-30|=30.
$$

Scaling two different edges multiplies their scale factors; it does not add or square them.

:question/problem:
Find $k$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{a}=\langle k,1,1\rangle$, $\mathbf{b}=\langle 1,0,1\rangle$, and $\mathbf{c}=\langle 0,1,2\rangle$ are coplanar.

The first-row expansion of their scalar triple product is provided:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})&=k(0\cdot2-1\cdot1)\\
&\quad -(1\cdot2-1\cdot0)\\
&\quad +(1\cdot1-0\cdot0).
\end{aligned}
$$

Select the value of $k$.
:question/worked-solution:
Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero. Simplify the supplied expansion:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})&=k(0-1)-(2-0)+(1-0)\\
&=-k-2+1\\
&=-k-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Set this equal to zero and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-k-1&=0\\
-k&=1\\
k&=-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the vectors are coplanar exactly when $k=-1$. At this value the triple product is $-(-1)-1=0$, so the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors has zero volume.

:question/problem:
Find $t$ given that the vectors $\mathbf{p}=\langle t,2,t\rangle$, $\mathbf{q}=\langle 1,2,-1\rangle$, and $\mathbf{r}=\langle 2,1,3\rangle$ are coplanar.

$t=${{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
The vectors are coplanar if and only if $\mathbf{p}\cdot(\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{r})=0$. Compute the triple product as a determinant, expanding along its first row:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{p}\cdot(\mathbf{q}\times\mathbf{r})
&=\begin{vmatrix}t&2&t\\1&2&-1\\2&1&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&=t\begin{vmatrix}2&-1\\1&3\end{vmatrix}
-2\begin{vmatrix}1&-1\\2&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +t\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=t(2\cdot3-(-1)\cdot1)-2(1\cdot3-(-1)\cdot2)\\
&\quad +t(1\cdot1-2\cdot2)\\
&=7t-10-3t\\
&=4t-10.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both occurrences of $t$ contribute to the equation. Setting the triple product equal to zero gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
4t-10&=0\\
4t&=10\\
t&=\frac{5}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vectors are coplanar exactly when $t=\frac{5}{2}$. Substitution gives $4\cdot\frac{5}{2}-10=0$.

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero. Expanding along the first row gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})
&=\begin{vmatrix}3&k^2&3\\1&3&2\\2&-1&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=3\begin{vmatrix}3&2\\-1&1\end{vmatrix}
-k^2\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +3\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\2&-1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=3(3\cdot1-2\cdot(-1))-k^2(1\cdot1-2\cdot2)\\
&\quad +3(1\cdot(-1)-3\cdot2)\\
&=3(5)-k^2(-3)+3(-7)\\
&=15+3k^2-21\\
&=3k^2-6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Set the triple product equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3k^2-6&=0\\
3k^2&=6\\
k^2&=2\\
k&=\pm\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both signs must be retained because either value has square $2$. In ascending order, the values are $-\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2}$. For each, the triple product is $3(2)-6=0$, so both make the vectors coplanar.

:question/problem:
Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\overrightarrow{AD}$, given

$$
A(1,-1,2),\quad B(2,1,2),\quad C(0,0,4),\quad D(3,-1,3).
$$

Select the volume in cubic units.
:question/worked-solution:
First find the displacement vectors from the common vertex $A$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}&=\langle2-1,1-(-1),2-2\rangle=\langle1,2,0\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AC}&=\langle0-1,0-(-1),4-2\rangle=\langle-1,1,2\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AD}&=\langle3-1,-1-(-1),3-2\rangle=\langle2,0,1\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $T=\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD})$. Expand its determinant along the first row. The cofactor signs are $+,-,+$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+0\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}\\
&=1(1\cdot1-2\cdot0)-2((-1)\cdot1-2\cdot2)+0\\
&=1-2(-5)\\
&=11.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
V=|11|=11\text{ cubic units}.
$$

Both nonzero cofactor contributions are needed. The middle contribution is positive because the cofactor sign and its minor are both negative. There is no division by six: that factor would give a tetrahedron's volume.

:question/problem:
Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\overrightarrow{AD}$, given

$$
A(3,1,1),\quad B(1,1,1),\quad C(4,4,1),\quad D(3,2,3).
$$

First subtract the coordinates of $A$ from each endpoint to find the three edge vectors. Then use

$$
V=\left|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\left(\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD}\right)\right|.
$$

The schematic shows the three edges meeting at a common vertex, with $\mathbf{a}=\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\mathbf{b}=\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\mathbf{c}=\overrightarrow{AD}$.

![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)

Select the volume in cubic units.
:question/worked-solution:
Form each displacement vector by subtracting the common starting point $A$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}&=\langle 1-3,1-1,1-1\rangle=\langle-2,0,0\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AC}&=\langle 4-3,4-1,1-1\rangle=\langle1,3,0\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AD}&=\langle 3-3,2-1,3-1\rangle=\langle0,1,2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

The scalar triple product is the determinant with these edge vectors as rows. Expanding along the first row, the two zero entries leave just one term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD})
&=\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-2)(3\cdot2-0\cdot1)\\
&=-12.
\end{aligned}
$$

Volume is the absolute value of the triple product, so

$$
V=|-12|=12\text{ cubic units}.
$$

The negative triple product describes orientation; it does not give a negative volume. Using the position vectors of $B$, $C$, and $D$ without subtracting $A$ would give the wrong edges.

:question/problem:
Calculate the volume $V$ of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB}$, $\overrightarrow{AC}$, and $\overrightarrow{AD}$, given

$$
A(-1,2,-1),\quad B(1,1,0),\quad C(0,3,0),\quad D(0,4,-3).
$$

Enter the volume in cubic units.

$V=$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Subtract $A$ from each endpoint to obtain the three edge vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{AB}&=\langle1-(-1),1-2,0-(-1)\rangle=\langle2,-1,1\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AC}&=\langle0-(-1),3-2,0-(-1)\rangle=\langle1,1,1\rangle,\\
\overrightarrow{AD}&=\langle0-(-1),4-2,-3-(-1)\rangle=\langle1,2,-2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $T=\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AD})$. All three first-row cofactor contributions are nonzero:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\\
&=2(1\cdot(-2)-1\cdot2)\\
&\quad{}-(-1)(1\cdot(-2)-1\cdot1)\\
&\quad{}+1(1\cdot2-1\cdot1)\\
&=2(-4)+(-3)+1\\
&=-8-3+1\\
&=-10.
\end{aligned}
$$

The required volume is the absolute value:

$$
V=|-10|=10\text{ cubic units}.
$$

Using the endpoint position vectors instead of the displacement vectors changes the solid. Taking the absolute value of each cofactor term separately is also incorrect: combine the signed contributions before taking the absolute value.

The volume is the absolute value of the scalar triple product of the actual edge vectors. Use those edges as the determinant rows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\begin{vmatrix}-4&-1&3\\2&0&-4\\-3&3&4\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-4)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0&-4\\3&4\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad -(-1)\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2&-4\\-3&4\end{vmatrix}\\
&\quad +3\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2&0\\-3&3\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-4)(0\cdot 4-(-4)\cdot 3)\\
&\quad -(-1)(2\cdot 4-(-4)\cdot (-3))\\
&\quad +3(2\cdot 3-0\cdot (-3))\\
&=(-48)+(-4)+18=-34.
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, take the absolute value:

$$
V=|-34|=34.
$$

T&=\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Expand along row $1$, whose cofactor signs are $+,-,+$. Zero entries make no contribution. Evaluate the needed minors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_1&=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(-1)\cdot(-1)-(-1)\cdot(-2)=-1\\
M_2&=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix}\\

M_3&=\begin{vmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\\

\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}
T&=3M_1+2M_2+(-1)M_3\\

\end{aligned}

$$

\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

Expand along row $1$, whose cofactor signs are $+,-,+$. Zero entries make no contribution. Evaluate the needed minors:

$$

$$

Given ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = \sin   ( y ) ,$ find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y = y(x).$

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} ) &  = \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( \sin   ( y ) ) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( {x}^{2} ) + \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( {y}^{2} ) &  = \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} x} ( \sin   ( y ) ) \\ 2 x + 2 y \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = \cos   ( y ) \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x}\end{array}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}2 x + 2 y \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = \cos   ( y ) \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} \\ 2 y \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} - \cos   ( y ) \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = - 2 x \\ ( 2 y - \cos   ( y ) ) \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = - 2 x \\ \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = - \frac{2 x}{2 y - \cos   ( y )} \\ \frac{\text{d} y}{\text{d} x} &  = \frac{2 x}{\cos   ( y ) - 2 y}\end{array}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(1,\,2 \right)$ for the curve $xy+y^2=2x^2+4.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y = y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+4) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x \\ (x+2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4x-y}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(1,\,2 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
m
&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\\[5pt]
&=\left(\dfrac{4x-y}{x+2y}\right)_{\left(1,\,2 \right)}\\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{4\cdot 1-2}{1+2\cdot 2}\\[5pt]
&=\dfrac{2}{5} \, .
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
The equation $x^2-2x+y^2+4y=5$ represents a circle. The normal line at the point $\left(0, -5 \right)$ on the circle intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

![](images/b6/b6c52a76654a4a545d356890d4deb04c74301e4091422a51e84551aeb3ec1152.png)
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(0,-5).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, $m',$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m' = -\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y = y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2-2x+ y^2+4y)
	&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (x^2)-\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (2x)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (y^2)+\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (4y)&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} (5)\\[5pt]	
	
	2x-2+2y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}+4\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=0\\[5pt]	
	
	
	(2y+4)\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=2-2x\\[5pt]	
	
	\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
	&=\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}
	
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}
	m
	&=\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\left(\dfrac{2-2x}{2y+4}\right)_{\left(0,\,-5 \right)}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2-2\cdot 0}{2\cdot (-5)+4}\\[5pt]
	&=\dfrac{2}{-6}\\[5pt]
	&=-\dfrac{1}{3} \, .
	
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $m'=-\dfrac{1}{m}=3.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $\left(0,\,-5 \right)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y-y_1 &=m'\left(x-x_1 \right)\\[5pt]
	y+5 &=3\left(x-0 \right)\\[5pt]
	y&=3x-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
	y&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	0&=3x-5\\[5pt]
	x&=\dfrac{5}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{5}{3},\,0 \right).$

:question/problem: Given $xy+y^2=x^2,$ find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y = y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ (x+2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x-y}{x+2y}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2}, 1)$ for the curve $x^{2} + 4y^{2} = 6$.
:question/worked-solution: Implicit differentiation gives $2x+8y\,y'=0$, so $y'=-x/(4y)$ wherever $y\ne0$. At $(\sqrt2,1)$, the slope is $$-\frac{\sqrt2}{4}=-\frac1{2\sqrt2}.$$

:question/problem: Given that $\cos y + 2x^{2} - y = 10x$, calculate $\frac{dy}{dx}$.
:question/worked-solution: Differentiate implicitly: $$-\sin y\,y'+4x-y'=10.$$ Solving for the derivative gives $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4x-10}{1+\sin y}=\frac{2(2x-5)}{\sin y+1},$$ where the denominator is nonzero.

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for $xy + y^{2} = 3x^{2}$.
:question/worked-solution: Apply the product and chain rules: $y+xy'+2yy'=6x$. Thus $$(x+2y)y'=6x-y\implies\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{6x-y}{x+2y},$$ where $x+2y\ne0$.

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)=2x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\ [(x)(\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{dy}}{\text{d}x})+(1)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y))] & =2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) & =2 \\ \frac{x}{y}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y(2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y))}{x}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}=-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+xy-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2x+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y-2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ (2x+y)+(x-2y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x-2y}\right)}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 0+1}{0-2\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{0+1}{0-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)=8{x}^{3}.$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y) & =8{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}) \\ [({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{dy}}{\text{d}x})+(2x)(\operatorname{ln}(y))] & =24{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)+2x\operatorname{ln}(y) & =24{x}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =24{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y(24{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}(y))}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =24y-\frac{2y\operatorname{ln}(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3}=8x.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3} & =8x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x) \\ [{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy]-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-12{y}^{2}) & =8-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{8-2xy}{{x}^{2}-12{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\,2)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}=2.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3})+{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{3}\cdot 2x & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2y}{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\,2)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1/2,\,2)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2y}{3x}\right)}_{(1/2,\,2)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 2}{3\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ for the curve $y\operatorname{cos}(x)=1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $y\operatorname{cos}(x)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\operatorname{cos}(x)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}(x))+\operatorname{cos}(x)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y) & =0 \\ y(-\operatorname{sin}(x))+\operatorname{cos}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{sin}(x) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y\operatorname{sin}(x)}{\operatorname{cos}(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(0,\,1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & ={\frac{y\operatorname{sin}(x)}{\operatorname{cos}(x)}}_{(0,\,1)} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot \operatorname{sin}(0)}{\operatorname{cos}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 0}{1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $xy+{x}^{2}=1.$ The normal line at the point $(1,\,0)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(1,\,0).$   Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy+{x}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y+2x & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-(2x+y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x+y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,0)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2x+y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,0)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 1+0}{1} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $$
\displaystyle {m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{-2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(1,\,0)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-0) & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}(0-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,-\frac{1}{2}).$

The equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$  represents a circle. The tangent line at the point $(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})$ on the circle intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2}).$ 

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x}{2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})$  is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{x}{y}\right)}_{(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},\,\sqrt{2})$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-\sqrt{2}) & =-1(x-\sqrt{2}) \\ y & =-(x-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(x-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =-(0-\sqrt{2})+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2} \\ y & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,2\sqrt{2}).$

$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2y+1) & =4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4}{2y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x+7}+\sqrt{y+2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((x+7)^{1/2}+(y+2)^{1/2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6) \\ \frac{1}{2}(x+7)^{-1/2}+\frac{1}{2}(y+2)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(y+2)^{-1/2}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2}(x+7)^{-1/2} \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y+2}}\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+7}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\sqrt{y+2}}{\sqrt{x+7}}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\,7)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(2,\,7)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{\sqrt{y+2}}{\sqrt{x+7}}\right)|}_{(2,\,7)} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{7+2}}{\sqrt{2+7}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{3}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}y & =4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4x) \\ 3{x}^{2}y+{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 \\ {x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4-3{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4-3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,4)$ is then given by

:question/problem:
The equation of a curve is $8y={x}^{2}+4x.$ The normal line at the point $(4,4)$ intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}8y & ={x}^{2}+4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4x) \\ 8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+4}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{x+2}{4}\right)|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$

$$

We can write the equation of the normal line at the point $(4,4)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-4) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{8}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}

:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}=9.$ The normal line at the point $(3,\,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,\,3).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 6x-4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-6x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-6x}{-4y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3x}{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,\,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{3x}{2y}\right)}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is $$
\displaystyle {m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3/2}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(3,\,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-3) & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(0-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(-3)+3 \\ y & =2+3 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

$$

$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{3},\,2)$ is then given by

$$

:question/problem: The equation of a curve is $2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}=8.$ The tangent line at the point $(1,\,1)$ on the curve intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\,1).$  

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 4x+12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 12y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-4x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{12y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{x}{3y}\right)}_{(1,\,1)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3\cdot 1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(1,1)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-1) & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-1)+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}(0-1)+1 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,\frac{4}{3}).$

$$

We can write the equation of the tangent line at the point $(2,8)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =-2(x-2) \\ y-8 & =-2x+4 \\ y & =-2x+12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-2x+12 \\ 2x & =12 \\ x & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(6,\,0).$

:question/problem:
![](images/0c/0c89b1d28ce7692f54e0fbf32c1d99b091e24729c837883523d6150450decb17.png)

The equation $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=20x$ represents an ellipse. The tangent line at the point $(4,4)$ on the ellipse intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

The coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the tangent line at the point $(4,4).$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(20x) \\ 8x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{20-8x}{2y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{10-4x}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={\left(\frac{10-4x}{y}\right)|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{10-4\cdot 4}{4} \\  & =\frac{(-6)}{4} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can write the equation of the tangent at the point $(4,4)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}(x-4)+4 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this tangent line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{2}x+10 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot 0+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,10).$

The equation $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=15y$ represents an ellipse. The normal line at the point $(3,3)$ on the ellipse intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P.$ What are the coordinates of $P?$

The coordinates of $P$ are $($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
:question/worked-solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,3).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{′},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =15y \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(15y) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(15y) \\ 8x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =15\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-15\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-8x \\ (2y-15)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-8x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{8x}{2y-15}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{8x}{2y-15}\right)|}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =-\frac{8\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3-15} \\  & =-\frac{24}{(-9)} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)}=-\frac{3}{8}.
$$

We can write the equation of the normal line at the point $(3,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{′}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{3}{8}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{9}{8}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $x$-axis. At the point $P$ the $y$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $y=0$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8} \\ 0 & =-\frac{3}{8}x+\frac{33}{8} \\ \frac{3}{8}x & =\frac{33}{8} \\ x & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(11,\,0).$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}y=-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-1) \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)+y\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2y}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(1,\,-1)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{2y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,-1)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot (-1)}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ for the curve $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)=\sqrt{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{2}) \\ x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) & =0 \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{4})$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(y)}{x}\right)}_{(2,\pi /4)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xy) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5) \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y & =0 \\ x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-y}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{y}{x}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & ={\left(-\frac{y}{x}\right)}_{(1,\,5)} \\  & =-\frac{5}{1} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}=2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(y))+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)]+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}) & =6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(y)}{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y)+3{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $x{e}^{y}={x}^{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $x{e}^{y}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x{e}^{y}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ [(x)({e}^{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+(1)({e}^{y})] & =2x \\ x\,{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{y} & =2x\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{e}^{y} & =2x \\ x{e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x-{e}^{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x-{e}^{y}}{x{e}^{y}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}y+4y=2{x}^{3}.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y+4y & =2{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y+4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}) \\ [{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x]+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4) & =6{x}^{2}-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{6{x}^{2}-2xy}{{x}^{2}+4}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $2xy+4{y}^{3}={x}^{2}-1.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $2xy$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+4{y}^{3} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2xy+4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2xy)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-1) \\ [2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y]+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x-2y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2x+12{y}^{2}) & =2x-2y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x-2y}{2x+12{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x-y}{x+6{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for $2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2}=4{x}^{2}+6.$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the $2{x}^{3}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2} & =4{x}^{2}+6 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}y+2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+6) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}y)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{2}+6) \\ [2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 6{x}^{2}]+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x \\ 2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{2}y+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8x-6{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+4y) & =8x-6{x}^{2}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{8x-6{x}^{2}y}{2{x}^{3}+4y}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ for $xy+y^2=2x^2+1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$ and write $y'=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$. The product rule gives $(xy)'=y+xy'$, and the chain rule gives $(y^2)'=2yy'$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+xy'+2yy'&=4x\\
xy'+2yy'&=4x-y\\
(x+2y)y'&=4x-y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing by the coefficient of $y'$ gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{4x-y}{x+2y},\qquad x+2y\ne0.
$$

:question/problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ for $x^2\sin y+y^2=xe^y+1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$ and write $y'=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. Both sides contain a product. Differentiate each product, retaining the chain-rule factor $y'$ when differentiating $\sin y$ or $e^y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^2\sin y)&=2x\sin y+x^2\cos y\,y',\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(xe^y)&=e^y+xe^y y'.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate the equation, then move every term containing $y'$ to the left and the other terms to the right:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x\sin y+x^2\cos y\,y'+2yy'&=e^y+xe^y y'\\
x^2\cos y\,y'+2yy'-xe^y y'&=e^y-2x\sin y\\
(x^2\cos y+2y-xe^y)y'&=e^y-2x\sin y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{e^y-2x\sin y}{x^2\cos y+2y-xe^y}.
$$

This formula applies where $x^2\cos y+2y-xe^y\ne0$.

:question/problem: Calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ for $x\sin y+y^2=x^3+1.$
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$ and write $y'=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$. Apply the product rule to $x\sin y$ and the chain rule to each function of $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x\sin y)&=\sin y+x\cos y\,y',\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(y^2)&=2yy'.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the equation and collecting the terms containing $y'$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin y+x\cos y\,y'+2yy'&=3x^2\\
x\cos y\,y'+2yy'&=3x^2-\sin y\\
(x\cos y+2y)y'&=3x^2-\sin y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{3x^2-\sin y}{x\cos y+2y},\qquad x\cos y+2y\ne0.
$$

:question/problem: Given that $y^2-3x+y=1$, calculate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function $y(x)$. The chain rule gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(y^2)=2y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(y^2-3x+y)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(1)\\
2y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-3+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Collect the terms containing $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$, factor, and divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=3\\
(2y+1)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=3\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{3}{2y+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This formula applies where $2y+1\ne 0$.

:question/problem: Given that $2^y-y=x^2+1$, calculate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function $y(x)$. For the exponential term, use the general-base rule together with the chain rule:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2^y)=2^y\ln(2)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2^y-y)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^2+1)\\
2^y\ln(2)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=2x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Factor out $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2^y\ln(2)-1)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=2x\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{2x}{2^y\ln(2)-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This formula applies where $2^y\ln(2)-1\ne 0$.

:question/problem: Given that $y^3+\cos(y)-x^2=2$, calculate $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function $y(x)$. Both $y^3$ and $\cos(y)$ require a factor of $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ from the chain rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(y^3+\cos(y)-x^2)&=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2)\\
3y^2\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-\sin(y)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-2x&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Collect and factor the terms containing $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3y^2\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}-\sin(y)\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=2x\\
(3y^2-\sin(y))\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=2x\\
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}&=\frac{2x}{3y^2-\sin(y)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This formula applies where $3y^2-\sin(y)\ne 0$.

Treat $y$ as a function of $x$. The term $xe^{xy}$ needs the product rule. Inside the exponential, $xy$ also needs the product rule:

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx},\qquad
\frac{d}{dx}(e^{xy})=e^{xy}\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right).
$$

Differentiate the curve and collect all terms containing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(xe^{xy}+y^2)&=\frac{d}{dx}(e+1)\\
e^{xy}+xe^{xy}\left(y+x\frac{dy}{dx}\right)+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=0\\
e^{xy}+xye^{xy}+x^2e^{xy}\frac{dy}{dx}+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=0\\
(x^2e^{xy}+2y)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-e^{xy}(1+xy)\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{e^{xy}(1+xy)}{x^2e^{xy}+2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(1,1)$, $e^{xy}=e$ and the denominator $e+2$ is positive. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,1)}\\
&=-\frac{e(1+1)}{e+2}\\
&=-\frac{2e}{e+2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$. Use the product rule on $xy$ and the chain rule on $y^2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(xy+y^2)&=\frac{d}{dx}(x^2-1)\\
x\frac{dy}{dx}+y+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=2x\\
(x+2y)\frac{dy}{dx}&=2x-y\\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{2x-y}{x+2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(2,1)$, the denominator is $2+2(1)=4$, so the slope is finite. Substituting gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
m&=\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(2,1)}\\
&=\frac{2(2)-1}{2+2(1)}\\
&=\frac{3}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem:
The equation of a curve is $xy+y^2=6$. The normal line at $(1,2)$ on the curve intersects the $y$-axis at $P$. Find the coordinates of $P$. Give exact values.

The coordinates of $P$ are $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Differentiate with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a function of $x$. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=y+x\frac{dy}{dx}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y\frac{dy}{dx}&=0 \\
(x+2y)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-y \\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{y}{x+2y}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope at $(1,2)$ is

$$
m_{\mathrm{t}}=-\frac{2}{1+2(2)}=-\frac{2}{5}.
$$

The normal slope is its negative reciprocal:

$$
m_{\mathrm{n}}=-\frac{1}{m_{\mathrm{t}}}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The normal through $(1,2)$ has equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-2&=\frac{5}{2}(x-1) \\
y&=\frac{5}{2}x-\frac{1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Set $x=0$ for the $y$-axis intersection. Then $y=-\frac{1}{2}$, giving

$$
P=\left(0,-\frac{1}{2}\right).

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Substitute and simplify:

\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $P=\left(18,0\right)$.

:question/problem:
The curve has equation $x^{2} + 4 y^{2}=68$. The **tangent** line at $\left(2,-4\right)$ meets the $y$-axis at $P$. Find the coordinates of $P$.

Use $y-y_0=m(x-x_0)$ with the given point. On the $y$-axis, $x=0$.

The curve has equation $3 x^{2} + 3 y^{2}=30$. The **tangent** line at $\left(-3,1\right)$ meets the $x$-axis at $P$. Find the coordinates of $P$.

Use $y-y_0=m(x-x_0)$ with the given point. On the $x$-axis, $y=0$.
:question/worked-solution:
Treat $y$ as a function of $x$. Differentiate implicitly and collect the derivative terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
6 x+\left(6 y\right)\frac{dy}{dx}&=0 \\
\left(6 y\right)\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\left(6 x\right) \\
\frac{dy}{dx}&=-\frac{6 x}{6 y}
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope at the given point:

$$
m_{\mathrm{t}}=-\frac{-18}{6}=3
$$

The tangent line uses $m=3$.

Use the given point and this slope:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-\left(1\right)&=3\left(x-\left(-3\right)\right) \\
y&=3\left(x-\left(-3\right)\right)+\left(1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Substitute and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=3\left(x-\left(-3\right)\right)+\left(1\right) \\
x-\left(-3\right)&=-\frac{1}{3} \\
x&=- \frac{10}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore $P=\left(- \frac{10}{3},0\right)$.

:question/problem:

$$

The vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}(t,z)$ above parametrizes the elliptic cylinder defined in Cartesian coordinates as $\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1.$ What is the first component of $\mathbf{f}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1$ in $xy$-plane has the parametrization

$$
\langle x,y \rangle = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 4\sin{t} \big\rangle,
\qquad t \in [0,2\pi),
$$

since 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}{4}+\frac{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{16} \\  & =\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4}+\frac{16{sin}^{2}⁡t}{16} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for any point $(x,y,z)$ on our surface, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{f}(t,z) & =⟨x,y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨{\color{blue}2\operatorname{cos}t},\hspace{0.222em}4\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in [0,2\pi)$ and $z \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Therefore, the first component of $\mathbf{f}$ is ${\color{blue}2\cos{t}}.$

$$

$$

:question/problem:
The function

$$
\mathbf f(t,z)=\langle \text{_____},\,3\tan t,\,z\rangle
$$

with $-\pi/2<t<\pi/2$ and $z\in\mathbb R$ parametrizes the sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder

$$
\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{9}=1,\qquad x\ge 2.
$$

Use $\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t=1$ and $\sec t\ge 1$ on this interval. What is the first component of $\mathbf f$?
:question/worked-solution:
The free coordinate $z$ controls movement parallel to the cylinder's axis. In the $xy$-plane, substituting $y=3\tan t$ gives

$$
\frac{x^2}{4}=1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t.
$$

Since $x\ge 2$ and $\sec t\ge 1$ on the given interval, choose the positive root: $x=2\sec t$. Thus

$$
\mathbf f(t,z)=\langle 2\sec t,\,3\tan t,\,z\rangle.
$$

Substitution verifies the equation:

$$
\frac{(2\sec t)^2}{4}-\frac{(3\tan t)^2}{9}
=\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t=1.
$$

As $t$ runs through $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$, $3\tan t$ takes every real value and $2\sec t$ gives the corresponding point on the positive branch. Letting $z$ range over all real numbers gives the whole sheet. The first component is $2\sec t$.

:question/problem:
The function

$$
\mathbf f(x,t)=\langle x,\,\text{_____},\,\sqrt{2}\tan t\rangle
$$

with $-\pi/2<t<\pi/2$ and $x\in\mathbb R$ parametrizes the sheet of the hyperbolic cylinder

$$
2y^2-3z^2=6,\qquad y\ge\sqrt{3}.
$$

What is the second component of $\mathbf f$?
:question/worked-solution:
Divide the Cartesian equation by $6$ to identify the two squared scale factors:

$$
\frac{y^2}{3}-\frac{z^2}{2}=1.
$$

The cross-section lies in the $yz$-plane and $x$ is free. With $z=\sqrt{2}\tan t$, the normalized equation gives

$$
\frac{y^2}{3}=1+\frac{(\sqrt{2}\tan t)^2}{2}
=1+\tan^2 t=\sec^2 t.
$$

The scale for $y$ is $\sqrt{3}$, not $3$. Since $\sec t\ge 1$ on the given interval and $y\ge\sqrt{3}$, the correct sign is positive:

$$
y=\sqrt{3}\sec t.
$$

Hence

$$
\mathbf f(x,t)=\langle x,\,\sqrt{3}\sec t,\,\sqrt{2}\tan t\rangle.
$$

Check directly in the original equation:

$$
2(\sqrt{3}\sec t)^2-3(\sqrt{2}\tan t)^2
=6(\sec^2 t-\tan^2 t)=6.
$$

The tangent coordinate takes every real $z$, the secant coordinate supplies the corresponding positive $y$, and arbitrary real $x$ extends this branch along the cylinder's axis. The second component is $\sqrt{3}\sec t$.

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the circle shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Since our circle is centered at $(0,-1)$ and has a radius of $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
(x-0)^2 + (y - (-1))^2 = 2^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x^2 + (y+1)^2 = 4.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+(y+1)^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((y+1)^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2(y+1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
:question/worked-solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $2$ and $4,$ its equation is given by

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{4^2} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{x^2}{4} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}\right)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}\right) & =0 \\ \frac{2x}{4}+\frac{2y}{16}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y}{8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{4x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(3,-2).$

The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
y^2 = 4px.
$$

Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)^{2} & =4p(3) \\ 4 & =12p \\ p & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
y^2 = \dfrac{4}{3}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{3}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Given that the point $(2,\sqrt{5})$ lies on the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ find ${f}^{″}(2).$

${f}^{″}(2)\,=\,$ {{field-1}}
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that 

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({f}^{′}(x))
$$

is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x).$ 

Notice that the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ on $x\in [-3,3]$ is a semicircle of a radius $3$ centered at $(0,0).$ Its equation (for $y>0$) is given by

$$
(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}={3}^{2}\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 2x+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(2) & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(2,\,\sqrt{5})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{{(-1-3)}^{2}+{(2-4)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\left( \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2}, \dfrac {y_1+y_2}{2}\right) = \left( \dfrac{3+(-1)}{2}, \dfrac {4+2}{2}\right)=(1,3)

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^{2}+(y-b)^{2} & ={r}^{2} \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & =(\sqrt{5})^{2} \\ (x-1)^{2}+(y-3)^{2} & =5\end{aligned}

The line segment $\overline{XY}$ is a diameter of a circle. Given that $X$ and $Y$ have coordinates $(-2,4)$ and $(-6,4)$, respectively, what is the equation of the circle?
:question/worked-solution:
The general equation of a circle with radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ is

$$
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2.
$$

Using the distance formula to compute the distance between the points $X(-2,4)$ and $Y(-6,4),$ we find that the length of the diameter is

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{((-2)-(-6))^2+(4-4)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^2+(0)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{16+0} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So the radius of the circle is

$$
r=\frac{XY}{2}=\frac{4}{2}=2.
$$

Since the center of a circle is the midpoint of the diameter, to find the center we use the midpoint formula as follows:

$$
(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2})=(\frac{-2+(-6)}{2},\frac{4+4}{2})=(-4,4)
$$

So our circle has radius $r=2$ and center $(a,b)=(-4,4),$ and therefore it is represented by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 & =r^2 \\ (x-(-4))^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =(2)^2 \\ (x+4)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

1. $\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{c}$
2. $\mathbf{e}=2\mathbf{a}$
