:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz}$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k}$ for $t \in [0,\sqrt 2].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) =t^2\, \mathbf{i} + t \,\mathbf{j} + 1 \,\mathbf{k},$ then along the curve we have $x = t^2,$ $y = t,$ and $z=1.$  

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+1\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+0\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x}{yz},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{t\cdot 1}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u= 4t^2+1,$ $\textrm d u=8t\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{9}\frac{1}{8}{u}^{1/2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[{9}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[27-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot 26 \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Find an integral that is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf r(t)= \left \langle \cos t, \sin t \right\rangle$ for $t \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f5/f53d78debfec5f8c50e0f3a5947d2a36126e18c073d7b0cc4c59d506753059b3.png)

The path of integration is shown above. We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Here, we have $f(x,y) =  xy^3$. Along the path, we have $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t,$ and so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =f(\operatorname{cos}t,\operatorname{sin}t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}t\cdot (\operatorname{sin}t)^{3} \\  & ={\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t\operatorname{cos}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t\operatorname{cos}t\cdot 1\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{3}t\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\int\limits_C xy^3 \, \textrm{d}s = \int^{\pi/2}_{0} \sin^3 t \cos t \, \textrm{d}t .
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle\int\limits_{C}xy\,\textrm{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j}\,$ for $0\leq t\leq 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t) = 3t\,\mathbf{i}+4t\,\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y=4t.$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y) =xy,$ then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =3t\cdot 4t \\  & =12{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{2}\cdot 5\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =60{[\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20{[{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized 
 by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{2}-t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\sqrt{2}]?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+t,\hspace{0.167em}{t}^{2}-t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+t,$ and $y={t}^{2}-t.$ 

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =(2t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t+1)^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4t+1+4{t}^{2}-4t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}+2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{2}(x-y)$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\sqrt{2}[({t}^{2}+t)-({t}^{2}-t)] \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2\sqrt{2}t\cdot \sqrt{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

For a scalar line integral, substitute the parametrization and multiply by speed. Here $r'(t)=\langle2\sqrt t,t-1\rangle$, so $\|r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4t+(t-1)^2}=t+1$ on $[0,1]$. Also $3x=4t^{3/2}$. Thus $$\int_C3x\,ds=4\int_0^1(t^{5/2}+t^{3/2})\,dt=4\left(\frac27+\frac25\right)=\frac{96}{35}.$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_(C)(x^{2} + y^{2})ds,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=3(\operatorname{cos}t+t\operatorname{sin}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3(\operatorname{sin}t-t\operatorname{cos}t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}$ for $0 \le t \le 2π$.
:question/worked-solution: Differentiating gives $r'(t)=3t\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangle$, so the speed is $3t$ on $[0,2\pi]$. Also $x^2+y^2=9(1+t^2)$. Hence $$\int_C(x^2+y^2)\,ds=27\int_0^{2\pi}(t+t^3)\,dt=54\pi^2+108\pi^4=54\pi^2(1+2\pi^2).$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $t\in [\sqrt{2},\sqrt{6}].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$, then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=t+1.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{12x}{y-1}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{(t+1)-1} \\  & =\frac{12{t}^{2}}{t} \\  & =12t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{6}}12t\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4{t}^{2}+1,$ $\text{d}u=8t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle \int_(C)4yz\cos xds,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\hspace{0.167em}$ for $0 < t < \frac{π}{2}$.
:question/worked-solution: Here $x=t$, $y=\sin t$, and $z=1$. The speed is $\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}$. Thus $$\int_C4yz\cos x\,ds=\int_0^{\pi/2}4\sin t\cos t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}\,dt.$$ Set $u=1+\cos^2t$, so $du=-2\sin t\cos t\,dt$. :question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$

$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}$ for $-1 \le t \le 2$?
:question/worked-solution: Substitute $x=2t$, $y=2-t$ to get $x^3-y=8t^3+t-2$. The speed is $\sqrt{2^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt5$. Therefore $$\int_C(x^3-y)\,ds=\sqrt5\int_{-1}^{2}(8t^3+t-2)\,dt.$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $0\le t\le 1?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ 

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2t\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{4y+1}$, then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{4y+1}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\frac{t}{4{t}^{2}+1}\right)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{t}{\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}1+t⟩$ for $t\in [0,1].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}1+t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=1+t.$    

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =t+(1+t)=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+1)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}2t+1\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{[{t}^{2}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1+1-0) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em},$ for $t\in [0,1].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$, then along the curve we have $x=3t$ and $y={t}^{3}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9{t}^{4}} \\  & =3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{3}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =(3t)^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =27{t}^{3}+{t}^{3} \\  & =28{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}28{t}^{3}\cdot 3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{4},$ $\text{d}u=4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}84{t}^{3}\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{2}21\cdot {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =21\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =14({2}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =14(2\sqrt{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+16{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-16$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}-16 \\  & =16(2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-1) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2{x}^{2}-16)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}16\operatorname{cos}2t\cdot 4\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =64{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}2t]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =32[\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}0] \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}t-1,\hspace{0.222em}t+1⟩$ for $t\in [0,3]?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}t-1,\hspace{0.222em}t+1⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2},$ $y=t-1,$ and $z=t+1.$ 

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\mathbf{k} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=2x-{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =2({t}^{2})-(t-1)^{2}-(t+1)^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-({t}^{2}-2t+1)-({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2}+2t-1-{t}^{2}-2t-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{4{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2(2{t}^{2}+1)}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2)\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$  

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if $f(x,y)={y}^{2}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}=4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\left(\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}2t}{2}\right)\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}2t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{[t-\frac{\operatorname{sin}2t}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4[(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})-0] \\  & =\pi -2.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}t-4⟩$ for $t\in [0,4].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨t,\hspace{0.222em}t-4⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=t$ and $y=t-4.$     

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-4)\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y-x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{1}{t-(4-t)}=-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{4}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}\cdot \hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{4}\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}t\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\cdot (4-0) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $C$ is the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=4{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $0\le t\le 1.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=4{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+3{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x=4{t}^{2}$ and $y=3{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\mathbf{j} \\  & =8t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+6t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8t)^{2}+(6t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{64{t}^{2}+36{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{100{t}^{2}} \\  & =10|t| \\  & =10t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{3}-2{y}^{3}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={(4{t}^{2})}^{3}-2{(3{t}^{2})}^{3} \\  & ={4}^{3}{t}^{6}-2\cdot {3}^{3}{t}^{6} \\  & =64{t}^{6}-54{t}^{6} \\  & =10{t}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{3}-{y}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10{t}^{6}\cdot 10t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =100{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{7}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =100\cdot \frac{{t}^{8}}{8}\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =100[\frac{{1}^{8}}{8}+\frac{{0}^{8}}{8}] \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1}{8} \\  & =12.5.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$  along the curve $C$ parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $0<t<\sqrt{\pi /2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)={t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j},$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-{t}^{2}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ because $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.167em}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,t\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}(1-0) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5},$ along the curve parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}-3\operatorname{sin}t⟩$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨4\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.222em}-3\operatorname{sin}t⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$   

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{r}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{cos}^{2}+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =\sqrt{25{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t} \\  & =5|\operatorname{cos}t| \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ because $\operatorname{cos}⁡t\ge 0$ when $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{5}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{16{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+9{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{5} \\  & =\frac{25{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t}{5} \\  & =5{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}5{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

   

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}25{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =25{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =25\cdot {\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =25(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{25}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $$
\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}
$$
for $1<t<\sqrt{2}.$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

 

Since $$
\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},
$$ then along the curve we have $x=t,$ $y=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2},$ and $z=\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{t}^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}}{t}=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y+z}{x}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+2{t}^{2}$, $\text{d}u=4t\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t\sqrt{1+2{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{3}^{5}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}({5}^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{5}-3\sqrt{3}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s,
$$ where $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$ and the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}-1,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2]?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}-1,\hspace{0.222em}{t}^{2}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x={t}^{2}+1,$ $y={t}^{2}-1,$ and $z={t}^{2}.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\mathbf{k} \\  & =2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}|t| \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t>0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x+y-z$, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =({t}^{2}+1)+({t}^{2}-1)-{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{2}-{t}^{2} \\  & ={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}t\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{t}^{3}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,
$$ where the curve $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\hspace{0.167em}+t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ then along the curve we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ and $z=t.$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t)\mathbf{j}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\mathbf{k} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k} \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, if $f(x,y,z)=z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =t((\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}-(\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}) \\  & =t({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t-{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}z({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\hspace{0.167em}‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}2t\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=- x - 3 y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $$
\displaystyle r(t)=⟨\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\,2 t^{2} - 4 t⟩
$$ for $t\in [0,2].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $$
\displaystyle r(t)=⟨\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3},\,2 t^{2} - 4 t⟩,
$$ then along the curve we have $x=\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}$ and $y=2 t^{2} - 4 t.$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t^{2} - 4 t)j \\ &=(8 \sqrt{t})i+(4 t - 4)j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(8 \sqrt{t})^2+(4 t - 4)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{64t+16(t-1)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{16(t^2+2t+1)} \\ &=4|t+1| \\ &=4 t + 4\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t+1|=t+1$ since $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=- x - 3 y$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=(-1)\left(\frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)+(-3)(2 t^{2} - 4 t) \\ &=- \frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 6 t^{2} + 12 t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C - x - 3 y\,\text{d}s&=\int_{0}^{2}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}(- \frac{16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 6 t^{2} + 12 t)\cdot (4 t + 4)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}- \frac{64}{3}t^{3/2}(t+1)+(-48)(t^2/2-t)(t+1)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{2}- \frac{64 t^{\frac{5}{2}}}{3} - \frac{64 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - 24 t^{3} + 24 t^{2} + 48 t\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[\left(- \frac{128 t^{\frac{7}{2}}}{21}\right)+\left(- \frac{128 t^{\frac{5}{2}}}{15}\right)+(- 6 t^{4})+(8 t^{3})+(24 t^{2})\right]_{0}^{2} \\ &=\left(\left(- \frac{128 (2)^{\frac{7}{2}}}{21}\right)+\left(- \frac{128 (2)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{15}\right)+(- 6 (2)^{4})+(8 (2)^{3})+(24 (2)^{2})\right)-\left(\left(- \frac{128 (0)^{\frac{7}{2}}}{21}\right)+\left(- \frac{128 (0)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{15}\right)+(- 6 (0)^{4})+(8 (0)^{3})+(24 (0)^{2})\right) \\ &=\left(\left(- \frac{1024 \sqrt{2}}{21}\right)+\left(- \frac{512 \sqrt{2}}{15}\right)+(-96)+(64)+(96)\right)-\left((0)+(0)+(0)+(0)+(0)\right) \\ &=64 - \frac{8704 \sqrt{2}}{105}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} - 3$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨5 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 5 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 5 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩$ for $t\in [1,3].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨5 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 5 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 5 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=5 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $y=- 5 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 5 \sin{\left(t \right)}.$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 5 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 5 \sin{\left(t \right)})j \\ &=(5)(-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t)i+(5)(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t)j \\ &=(5 t \cos{\left(t \right)})i+(5 t \sin{\left(t \right)})j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(5 t \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(5 t \sin{\left(t \right)})^2} \\ &=\sqrt{25t^2(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)} \\ &=5|t| \\ &=5 t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ since $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=2 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} - 3$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=(2)\left((5 t \sin{\left(t \right)} + 5 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 5 t \cos{\left(t \right)} + 5 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2\right)+(-3) \\ &=(50)\left(\cos^2t+2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\sin^2t+\sin^2t-2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\cos^2t\right)+(-3) \\ &=(50)(1+t^2)+(-3) \\ &=50 t^{2} + 47\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 2 x^{2} + 2 y^{2} - 3\,\text{d}s&=\int_{1}^{3}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{3}(50 t^{2} + 47)\cdot (5 t)\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{1}^{3}250 t^{3} + 235 t\,\text{d}t \\ &=\left[\left(\frac{235 t^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{125 t^{4}}{2}\right)\right]_{1}^{3} \\ &=\left(\left(\frac{235 (3)^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{125 (3)^{4}}{2}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{235 (1)^{2}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{125 (1)^{4}}{2}\right)\right) \\ &=\left(\left(\frac{2115}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{10125}{2}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{235}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{125}{2}\right)\right) \\ &=5940.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2 x + 2 y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨- 2 t,\,- 2 t - 2⟩$ for $t\in [-2,0].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨- 2 t,\,- 2 t - 2⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=- 2 t$ and $y=- 2 t - 2.$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 2 t - 2)j \\ &=(-2)i+(-2)j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-2)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{8} \\ &=2 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=2 x + 2 y$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=(2)\left(- 2 t+(- 2 t - 2)\right) \\ &=- 8 t - 4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C 2 x + 2 y\,\text{d}s&=\int_{-2}^{0}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{-2}^{0}(- 8 t - 4)\cdot (2 \sqrt{2})\,\text{d}t \\ &=(2 \sqrt{2})\int_{-2}^{0}- 8 t - 4\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{-2}^{0}- 16 \sqrt{2} t - 8 \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t \\ &=(4 \sqrt{2})\left[- 2 t^{2}+(- 2 t)\right]_{-2}^{0} \\ &=\left[(- 8 \sqrt{2} t^{2})+(- 8 \sqrt{2} t)\right]_{-2}^{0} \\ &=\left((- 8 \sqrt{2} (0)^{2})+(- 8 \sqrt{2} (0))\right)-\left((- 8 \sqrt{2} (-2)^{2})+(- 8 \sqrt{2} (-2))\right) \\ &=\left((0)+(0)\right)-\left((- 32 \sqrt{2})+(16 \sqrt{2})\right) \\ &=16 \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9 - 2 x^{2}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩$ for $t\in [- \frac{\pi}{2},- \frac{\pi}{4}].$
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t.
$$

Since $r(t)=⟨3 \cos{\left(t \right)},\,- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}⟩,$ then along the curve we have $x=3 \cos{\left(t \right)}$ and $y=- 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}.$

Computing $r^{\prime}(t)$ and $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=- 2 x - 2 y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨- t,\,1 - t⟩$ for $t\in [0,3].$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, if $f(x,y)=- 2 x - 2 y$, then we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=(-2)\left(- t+(1 - t)\right) \\ &=4 t - 2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C - 2 x - 2 y\,\text{d}s&=\int_{0}^{3}f(r(t))\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}(4 t - 2)\cdot (\sqrt{2})\,\text{d}t \\ &=(\sqrt{2})\int_{0}^{3}4 t - 2\,\text{d}t \\ &=\int_{0}^{3}4 \sqrt{2} t - 2 \sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t \\ &=(- 2 \sqrt{2})\left[- t^{2}+(t)\right]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left[(2 \sqrt{2} t^{2})+(- 2 \sqrt{2} t)\right]_{0}^{3} \\ &=\left((2 \sqrt{2} (3)^{2})+(- 2 \sqrt{2} (3))\right)-\left((2 \sqrt{2} (0)^{2})+(- 2 \sqrt{2} (0))\right) \\ &=\left((18 \sqrt{2})+(- 6 \sqrt{2})\right)-\left((0)+(0)\right) \\ &=12 \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}r^{\prime}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}j \\ &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{20 t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{5 t^{2}}{2} - 5 t)j \\ &=(10 \sqrt{t})i+(5 t - 5)j \\ \|r^{\prime}(t)\|&=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{(10 \sqrt{t})^2+(5 t - 5)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{100t+25(t-1)^2} \\ &=\sqrt{25(t^2+2t+1)} \\ &=5|t+1| \\ &=5 t + 5\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t+1|=t+1$ since $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x + 2 y$, then we obtain

$$

$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=- \frac{3}{- x + y}$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $r(t)=⟨3 t,\,3 t + 6⟩$ for $t\in [-2,2].$

$$

:question/problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9 y$ along the curve parametrized by $r(t)=\langle t^{2},t\rangle$ for $t\in [0,2 \sqrt{3}].$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t^{2})\,i+(t)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=t^{2}$, $y=t$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =(2 t)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9 y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(9)(t) \\  & =9 t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2 \sqrt{3}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2 \sqrt{3}}(9 t)(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4 t^{2} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(8 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2 \sqrt{3}}9 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{49}\frac{9}{8}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{1}^{49} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(49)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[(343)-(1)] \\  & =\left(\frac{1029}{4}\right)-\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{513}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=3 x y - 3 z^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t))&=3\left((t^{2})(2 t + 1)-(3 t + 1)^2\right) \\ &= 3\left(2t^3+(1)t^2-\left(9t^2+(6)t+1\right)\right) \\ &= 6 t^{3} - 24 t^{2} - 18 t - 3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

$$
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds,
$$

where

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,\sin t,1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le\frac\pi2.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar line integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Along the curve, $x=t$, $y=\sin t$, and $z=1$. Hence

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=3\sin t\cos t.
$$

Differentiate all three coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1,\cos t,0\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds
=\int_0^{\pi/2}3\sin t\cos t\sqrt{1+\cos^2t}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Choose $u=1+\cos^2t$. Then $\mathrm du=-2\sin t\cos t\,\mathrm dt$. The limits reverse:

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac\pi2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $1$ |

So

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C 3yz\cos x\,\mathrm ds
&=-\frac32\int_2^1 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac32\int_1^2 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^2\\
&=2\sqrt2-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The integrand is nonnegative on this interval, which also checks the sign.

:question/problem:

where

$$

$$

:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar function in three variables,

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Here $x=t$, $y=t^2/2$, and $z=t^2$. Since $t\ge1$, the denominator is nonzero, and

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=\frac{t^2/2+t^2}{t}=\frac32t.
$$

All three derivative components contribute to arc length:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1,t,2t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{1^2+t^2+(2t)^2}=\sqrt{1+5t^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\int_C\frac{y+z}{x}\,\mathrm ds
=\int_1^{\sqrt3}\frac32t\sqrt{1+5t^2}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

Choose $u=1+5t^2$, so $\mathrm du=10t\,\mathrm dt$ and $\frac32t\,\mathrm dt=\frac3{20}\,\mathrm du$. The transformed limits are

| $t$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $6$ | $16$ |

It follows that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C\frac{y+z}{x}\,\mathrm ds
&=\frac3{20}\int_6^{16}u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac1{10}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_6^{16}\\
&=\frac{64-6\sqrt6}{10}\\
&=\frac{32-3\sqrt6}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=6y$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t^2,t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

Use

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm ds=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm dt.
$$

For this curve, $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4t^2+1}$. Use the substitution $u=4t^2+1$ and give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
Along the curve, $x=t^2$ and $y=t$, so $f(\mathbf r(t))=6t$. The supplied speed follows from

$$
\mathbf r'(t)=\langle 2t,1\rangle,\qquad
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{(2t)^2+1^2}=\sqrt{4t^2+1}.
$$

Thus

$$
\int_C 6y\,\mathrm ds=\int_0^1 6t\sqrt{4t^2+1}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

With $u=4t^2+1$, we have $\mathrm du=8t\,\mathrm dt$ and $6t\,\mathrm dt=\frac34\,\mathrm du$. Change both limits:

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $5$ |

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C 6y\,\mathrm ds
&=\frac34\int_1^5 u^{1/2}\,\mathrm du\\
&=\frac12\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5\\
&=\frac{5\sqrt5-1}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to

$$
\int_C (xy+z)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$
where $\mathbf r(t)=\langle t^2+1,t^2-1,t^2\rangle$ for $-2\le t\le-1$?
:question/worked-solution:
Along the curve, $x=t^2+1$, $y=t^2-1$, and $z=t^2$. Compute the derivative and speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle2t,2t,2t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2t)^2+(2t)^2+(2t)^2}\\
&=\sqrt{12t^2}=2\sqrt{3}\,|t|.
\end{aligned}
$$

Every $t$ in $[-2,-1]$ is negative, so $|t|=-t$. Therefore the speed is $-2\sqrt{3}\,t$, which is positive on this interval.

Substitute into the scalar function, keeping the product grouped:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(t^2+1)(t^2-1)+t^2\\
&=t^4-1+t^2\\
&=t^4+t^2-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Combining these expressions, with the original parameter bounds, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (xy+z)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_{-2}^{-1}(t^4+t^2-1)(-2\sqrt{3}\,t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=-2\sqrt{3}\int_{-2}^{-1}t(t^4+t^2-1)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Using $2\sqrt{3}\,t$ as the speed would give a negative speed and the wrong sign for the integral.

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to

$$
\int_C (2x-y^2-z^2)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$
where $\mathbf r(t)=\langle t^2,t-2,t+2\rangle$ for $0\le t\le1$?
:question/worked-solution:
Here, $x=t^2$, $y=t-2$, and $z=t+2$.

First compute the derivative and speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle2t,1,1\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(2t)^2+1^2+1^2}=\sqrt{4t^2+2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute all three coordinates into the scalar function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=2t^2-(t-2)^2-(t+2)^2\\
&=2t^2-(t^2-4t+4)-(t^2+4t+4)\\
&=-8.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both squares are subtracted, including their constant terms. The scalar function is negative on the whole path, even though speed is nonnegative.

Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Combining the substituted function with the speed gives

$$
\int_C (2x-y^2-z^2)\,\mathrm{d}s=-8\int_0^1\sqrt{4t^2+2}\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

:question/problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to

$$
\int_C xy^2\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$
where $\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangle$ for $0\le t\le\pi/2$?
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f5/f53d78debfec5f8c50e0f3a5947d2a36126e18c073d7b0cc4c59d506753059b3.png)

The path is the quarter circle shown above. Along the curve, $x=\cos t$ and $y=\sin t$, so

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=\cos t\,(\sin t)^2=\sin^2 t\cos t.
$$

Differentiating the coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle-\sin t,\cos t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(-\sin t)^2+\cos^2 t}=1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Thus the equivalent definite integral is

$$
\int_C xy^2\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2 t\cos t\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The speed is $1$; no additional factor is needed.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2\cos t,2\sin t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

The path is the quarter circle of radius $2$ shown below.

![Quarter circle of radius 2 from (2,0) to (0,2), traversed counterclockwise.](images/6d/6d933c280ebb530aefaadc1b5ef927e39603635960348255045c138ee9bab366.png)

Along the curve, $x=2\cos t$ and $y=2\sin t$. Compute

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle -2\sin t,2\cos t\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{4\sin^2t+4\cos^2t}=2,\\
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(2\sin t)^2=4\sin^2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

The integral involves $\sin^2t$, so use the identity $\sin^2t=(1-\cos 2t)/2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}s
&=8\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=4\int_0^{\pi/2}(1-\cos 2t)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=4\left[t-\frac{\sin 2t}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}\\
&=4\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-0\right)=2\pi.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral

$$
\int_C (x^2+y^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2(\cos t+t\sin t),2(\sin t-t\cos t)\rangle.
$$

for $0\le t\le 1$.
:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Use the product rule in both components. The terms without a factor of $t$ cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x'(t)&=2(-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t)=2t\cos t,\\
y'(t)&=2(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t)=2t\sin t,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{4t^2\cos^2t+4t^2\sin^2t}\\
&=2|t|=2t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $|t|=t$ because $0\le t\le 1$. The speed is zero only at the starting endpoint.

Next, substitute both coordinates. Expanding the squares cancels the mixed terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(t)^2+y(t)^2
&=4\bigl[(\cos t+t\sin t)^2+(\sin t-t\cos t)^2\bigr]\\
&=4\bigl[\cos^2t+2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\sin^2t\\
&\qquad+\sin^2t-2t\sin t\cos t+t^2\cos^2t\bigr]\\
&=4(1+t^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(\mathbf r(t))=4(1+t^2)-2=2+4t^2$. Multiply this by the variable speed and integrate each term:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (x^2+y^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 (2+4t^2)\,2t\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\int_0^1 (4t+8t^3)\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=\left[2t^2+2t^4\right]_0^1\\
&=2+2=4.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=x+y$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2t,1+2t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a scalar line integral with respect to arc length, use

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Along the curve, $x=2t$ and $y=1+2t$. Differentiate the path and compute its speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 2,2\rangle,\\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{2^2+2^2}=2\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute the coordinates into the scalar function:

$$
f(\mathbf r(t))=2t+(1+2t)=1+4t.
$$

Multiply by the speed before integrating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}s
&=\int_0^1 (1+4t)\,2\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\\
&=2\sqrt{2}\left[t+2t^2\right]_0^1\\
&=2\sqrt{2}(1+2)=6\sqrt{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=- 2 \cos{\left(x \right)}$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 t^{2},- t^{2}\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{9}}.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(3 t^{2})\,i+(- t^{2})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=3 t^{2}$, $y=- t^{2}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- t^{2})\,j \\  & =(6 t)\,i+(- 2 t)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(6 t)^2+(- 2 t)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{40 t^{2}} \\  & =2 \sqrt{10}|t| \\  & =2 \sqrt{10} t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|t|=t$ because $t\geq0$ along the path of $C.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=- 2 \cos{\left(x \right)}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =- 2 \cos{\left(3 t^{2} \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{9}}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{9}}}(- 2 \cos{\left(3 t^{2} \right)})(2 \sqrt{10} t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=3 t^{2}$, $\text{d}u=(6 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}- \frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{3}\cdot \cos u\,\text{d}u \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{3}\sin u\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{3}[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)-\sin(0)] \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{10}}{3}[\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-(0)] \\  & =\left(- \frac{\sqrt{30}}{3}\right)-(0) \\  & =- \frac{\sqrt{30}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=\frac{x^{2}}{3} + \frac{y^{2}}{3}$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 \sin{\left(t \right)},- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)}\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\pi}{6}.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=3 \sin{\left(t \right)}$, $y=- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j \\  & =(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,i+(- 4 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(3 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 4 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{9\cos^2 t+16\cos^2 t} \\  & =\sqrt{25 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)}} \\  & =5|\cos t| \\  & =5 \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\cos t|=\cos t$ because $\cos t\geq0$ along this interval.

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{x^{2}}{3} + \frac{y^{2}}{3}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(3 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2+(- 4 \sin{\left(t \right)})^2}{3} \\  & =\frac{9\sin^2 t+16\sin^2 t}{3} \\  & =\frac{25 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\left(\frac{25 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)}}{3}\right)(5 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\frac{125 \sin^{2}{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}}{3}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\sin{\left(t \right)}$, $\text{d}u=(\cos{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{125}{3}\cdot u^2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{125}{3}\cdot\frac{u^3}{3}\big|_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{125}{3}[\frac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3}{3}-\frac{(0)^3}{3}] \\  & =\frac{125}{3}[\left(\frac{1}{24}\right)-(0)] \\  & =\left(\frac{125}{72}\right)-(0) \\  & =\frac{125}{72}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y,z)=6 y z \cos{\left(x \right)}$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t,2 \sin{\left(t \right)},1\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(t)\,i+(2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j+(1)\,k$, then along the curve we have $x=t$, $y=2 \sin{\left(t \right)}$, $z=1$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 \sin{\left(t \right)})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =(1)\,i+(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})\,j+(0)\,k \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(1)^2+(2 \cos{\left(t \right)})^2+(0)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

The substitution decreases from $5$ to $1$; its differential includes the negative sign.

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=6 y z \cos{\left(x \right)}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6)(2 \sin{\left(t \right)})(1)\cos(t) \\  & =12 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(12 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)})(\sqrt{4 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4 \cos^{2}{\left(t \right)} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(- 8 \sin{\left(t \right)} \cos{\left(t \right)})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{5}^{1}- \frac{3}{2}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =- \frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{5}^{1} \\  & =-1[(1)^{3/2}-(5)^{3/2}] \\  & =-1[(1)-(5 \sqrt{5})] \\  & =(-1)-(- 5 \sqrt{5}) \\  & =-1 + 5 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 2 t^{2},t\rangle,\qquad \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\le t\le \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(2 t^{2})\,i+(t)\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=2 t^{2}$, $y=t$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =(4 t)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(4 t)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{16 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1(2 t^{2})}{(t)-(0)} \\  & =\frac{2t^2}{t} \\  & =2 t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}}^{\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}}(2 t)(\sqrt{16 t^{2} + 1})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=16 t^{2} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(32 t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{9}^{25}\frac{1}{16}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{9}^{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}[(25)^{3/2}-(9)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{24}[(125)-(27)] \\  & =\left(\frac{125}{24}\right)-\left(\frac{9}{8}\right) \\  & =\frac{49}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral of $f(x,y)=x^{3} + 3 y$ along the curve

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle 3 t,t^{3}\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
$$

Give the exact value.
:question/worked-solution:
To calculate the line integral, we will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C f\,\text{d}s &=\int_a^b f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $r(t)=(3 t)\,i+(t^{3})\,j$, then along the curve we have $x=3 t$, $y=t^{3}$.

Computing $r'(t)$ and $\|r'(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r'(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3 t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{3})\,j \\  & =(3)\,i+(3 t^{2})\,j \\ \|r'(t)\| & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(3)^2+(3 t^{2})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{9 t^{4} + 9} \\  & =3 \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x^{3} + 3 y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3 t)^3+(3)(t^{3}) \\  & =27t^3+3t^3 \\  & =30 t^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =\int_C f\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\|r'(t)\|\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(30 t^{3})(3 \sqrt{t^{4} + 1})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}90 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 1$, $\text{d}u=(4 t^{3})\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{45}{2}\cdot u^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{45}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\big|_{1}^{2} \\  & =15[(2)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =15[(2 \sqrt{2})-(1)] \\  & =(30 \sqrt{2})-(15) \\  & =-15 + 30 \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

:question/problem:

:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral

$$
\int_C (- x - y)\,\mathrm{d}s,
$$

where $C$ is parametrized by

$$
\mathbf r(t)=\langle t, t - 2\rangle.
$$

The parameter interval is $0\leq t\leq 2$.
:question/worked-solution:
Use the scalar line-integral formula

$$
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))\,\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Differentiate both coordinates and compute the speed:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf r'(t)&=\langle 1, 1\rangle \\
\|\mathbf r'(t)\|&=\sqrt{(1)^2+(1)^2} \\
&=\sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$



Substitute the coordinates into the density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf r(t))&=(-1)\left((t)+(t - 2)\right) \\
&=2 - 2 t
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiply by the speed and integrate, subtracting the lower endpoint:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_C f\,\mathrm{d}s&=\int_{0}^{2} (2 - 2 t)\cdot (\sqrt{2})\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{2} - 2 \sqrt{2} t + 2 \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \sqrt{2} t^{2} + 2 \sqrt{2} t\right]_{0}^{2} \\
&=(0)-(0) \\
&=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x, y) =3x^2+4xy$ at the point $A(0,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,4).$
:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ \mathbf{u} & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{\mathbf{u}}^{'}(0,1) & =\mathrm{∇}g(0,1)\cdot \mathbf{u} \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f (x, y) = \ln (x^2y)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(2, 1)?$
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\mathrm{∇}f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}y))\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}y))\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot 2xy\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot {x}^{2}\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{y}\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\ -\mathrm{∇}f(2,1) & =-\frac{2}{2}\text{ }\mathbf{i}-\frac{1}{1}\text{ }\mathbf{j} \\  & =-\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $- \, \mathbf i - \mathbf j.$

:question/problem: Consider the function $g (x, y) = \ln \left(\sqrt {xy^3}\right).$ What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $$
\displaystyle \left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)\!\mathbin{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{3x{y}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2x},\,\frac{3}{2y}⟩ \\ ∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨\frac{1}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)},\frac{3}{2\cdot \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction of $$
\displaystyle \nabla g\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)
$$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})‖ & =‖⟨1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v}=5\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{29} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{29}}(5i+2j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇\,f(0,1) & =2\,i+(2\cdot 1)\,j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇\,f(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =(2i+2j)\cdot (\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}j) \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 5+2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{14\sqrt{29}}{29}.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,1)?$
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2xy-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{ }i+{x}^{2}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2\cdot 1\cdot 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\text{ }i+{1}^{2}\text{ }j \\  & =(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\text{ }i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\,i+j.$

:question/problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,1,2)?$
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z),\,2y,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1,2) & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2),\,2\cdot 1,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi ),\,2,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩.$

:question/problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(e,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)⟩ \\ ∇\,g(e,\pi ) & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)}{e},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡e\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{e},\,1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \cdot (-1)}{e},\,1\cdot (-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction of $∇g(e,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(e,\pi )‖ & =‖⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{{e}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}+{e}^{2}}}{e}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x, y) = (x + y^{2})^{2}$ at the point $A(-1,-2)$ in the direction towards the point $B(2, 2)$.

$$
\mathrm{∇}\hspace{-0.167em}f(1,1)=\mathrm{∇}(\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{V})\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{(1,\hspace{0.167em}1)}=4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\mathbf{u}}^{'}(1,1) & =\mathrm{∇}\hspace{-0.167em}f(1,1)\cdot \mathbf{u} \\  & =(4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+2\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\frac{1}{5}(-3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})) \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (-3)+2\cdot 4}{5} \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
