where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=(2x+y{e}^{z})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x{e}^{z}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(xy{e}^{z}-2z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{z}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{z}-2z & =xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{z}+{x}^{2}+y-{z}^{2}+C.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,i+2yz\,j+{y}^{2}\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{i}}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{j}}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{k}}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2yz)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) & ={y}^{2} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+{y}^{2}z+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f=\mathbf{F},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(2x{y}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2{x}^{2}y+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

$$

$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y) & =2{x}^{2}y+1 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =1 \\ g(y) & =y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+y+C.
$$

:question/problem:
Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ where $$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\left(\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (12{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{y})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{x}{{y}^{2}}+{g}^{′}(y) & =\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}} \\ g(y) & =\frac{1}{y}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=\frac{1}{y}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=3{x}^{4}-\frac{x}{y}+\frac{1}{y}+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ where $F(x,y,z)=(y+1)\,i+(x+z+1)\,j+(y+1)\,k.$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =xy+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+z+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x+z+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (z+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+x+yz+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+yz+x+y+z+C.
$$

:question/problem:

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z).$

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{i}}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{j}}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{\text{k}}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{xy} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z)$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(z) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3z) \\ h(z) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3z)+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f=\mathbf{F},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}y+\operatorname{sin}y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking  $$
\displaystyle \frac{∂f}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y
$$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y \\ g(y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(x{e}^{xy}+2y)\text{ }\mathbf{j}.$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{xy}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{xy}+2y$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{xy}+{g}^{′}(y) & =x{e}^{xy}+2y \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =2y \\ g(y) & ={y}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)={y}^{2}+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x{z}^{2}+z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2xyz+y-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=y{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y-2
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int y{z}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =xy{z}^{2}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{z}^{2}+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{z}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{z}^{2}+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int z\,\text{d}y \\  & =yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=2xyz+y-2$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xyz+y-2 & =2xyz+y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2 \\ h(z) & =-2z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{z}^{2}+yz-2z+C.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function

\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=2x{y}^{3}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z).$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{3}z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2x{y}^{3}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int {z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z) & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=(2x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2y+x+z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(y-2z)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2y+x+z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+x+z \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2y+z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (2y+z)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}+yz+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=y-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2z & =y+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy+{y}^{2}+yz-{z}^{2}+C.
$$

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\mathbf{F}(x,y),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=(3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\text{ }\mathbf{i}+(4-2xy)\text{ }\mathbf{j}.$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4-2xy
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}-x{y}^{2}+g(y)\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where $C$ is a constant.

:question/problem: Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\mathrm{∇}f(x,y,z)=\mathbf{F}(x,y,z),$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=4xy\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2{x}^{2}+2yz)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+({y}^{2}+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.$

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 4xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}y+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2{x}^{2}+2yz \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2yz\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 2yz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{2}z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)={y}^{2}z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={y}^{2}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+1 & ={y}^{2}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =1 \\ h(z) & =z+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+z+C.
$$

:question/problem:
Consider the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,z)&=\left(4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathbf{i} \\ &{}+\left(6 y z\right)\,\mathbf{j} \\ &{}+\left(3 y^{2}\right)\,\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
\nabla f(x,y,z)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathbf{i}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,\mathbf{j}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=6 y z \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=3 y^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=6 y z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=6 y z\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(6 y z\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=3 y^{2} z+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=3 y^{2} z+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=3 y^{2} z + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=3 y^{2}+h'(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=3 y^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3 y^{2}+h'(z)&=3 y^{2} \\ h'(z)&=0 \\ h(z)&=C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=3 y^{2} z + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}+C.
$$

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: f(x,y,z)=x e^{x y} + y e^{x y} + \cos{\left(2 z \right)}+C

$$

Since $\nabla f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}&=- 2 y - 2 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}&=- 2 x + 3 z + 3 \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=3 y + 3\end{aligned}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=\int \left(- 2 y - 2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x \\ &=- 2 x y - 2 x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=- 2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}.
$$

Taking $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=- 2 x + 3 z + 3$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}- 2 x+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=- 2 x + 3 z + 3 \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}&=3 z + 3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z)&=\int \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=\int \left(3 z + 3\right)\,\mathrm{d}y \\ &=3 y z + 3 y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=3 y z + 3 y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=- 2 x y - 2 x + 3 y z + 3 y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}=3 y+h'(z).
$$

$$
f(x,y,z)=- 2 x y - 2 x + 3 y z + 3 y + 3 z+C.

$$

$$
f(x,y,z)=x^2y+g(y,z).
$$

The integration term is a function of $y$ and $z$, since every term independent of $x$ vanishes when differentiated with respect to $x$. Differentiate with respect to $y$ and match the second component:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^2+g_y(y,z)&=x^2+2yz,\\
g_y(y,z)&=2yz,\\
g(y,z)&=y^2z+h(z).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f=x^2y+y^2z+h(z)$. The third component determines the remaining function:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_z&=y^2+h'(z),\\
y^2+h'(z)&=y^2-2z,\\
h'(z)&=-2z,\\
h(z)&=-z^2+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x^2y+y^2z-z^2+C.
$$

Checking all components gives $f_x=2xy$, $f_y=x^2+2yz$, and $f_z=y^2-2z$. Stopping after the first integration would miss the terms needed by the other two components.

\end{aligned}
$$

In the choices, $C$ is an arbitrary constant.
:question/worked-solution:
The components of $\nabla f$ are $f_x$ and $f_y$. Integrating $f_x$ with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as constant, leaves an arbitrary function $g(y)$ because its $x$-derivative is zero.

Integrating the first component term by term gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=\int\bigl(\cos(x+y)+2xy+y^2+2x\bigr)\,\mathrm dx\\
&=\sin(x+y)+x^2y+xy^2+x^2+g(y).
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, $\partial\sin(x+y)/\partial x=\cos(x+y)$ because $\partial(x+y)/\partial x=1$.

Now differentiate with respect to $y$:

$$
f_y=\cos(x+y)+x^2+2xy+g'(y).
$$

Match this with the second component. All three terms depending on $x$ cancel:

$$
\begin{aligned}
g'(y)&=\cos(x+y)+x^2+2xy+\sin y\\
&\quad-\bigl(\cos(x+y)+x^2+2xy\bigr)\\
g'(y)&=\sin y\\
g(y)&=-\cos y+C.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
f(x,y)=\sin(x+y)+x^2y+xy^2+x^2-\cos y+C.
$$

Checking both partial derivatives gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x&=\cos(x+y)+2xy+y^2+2x,\\
f_y&=\cos(x+y)+x^2+2xy+\sin y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Changing $-\cos y$ to $+\cos y$ passes the first-component check but reverses the sign of $\sin y$ in the second. Changing $+x^2$ to $-x^2$ passes the second-component check but reverses the sign of $2x$ in the first.

:question/problem: Let $\mathbf{a}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}$ and $\mathbf{b}={\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 1\end{array} \right]}.$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{u} & =\frac{\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}|}\end{aligned}$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+2\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2+2 \\ 0+(-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid a + 2b \mid &= \sqrt{0^{2} + (-2)^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{4} \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{u} & =\frac{\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}|} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}+2\mathbf{b}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}$$

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem: Let $r=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}$. Find a unit vector that is parallel to $r$ and points the same direction.
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
\begin{aligned}u &= \frac{r}{|r|}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|r| &= \sqrt{(6)^2+(8)^2} \\
&= \sqrt{100} \\
&= 10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $r$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u &= \frac{r}{|r|} \\
&= \frac{1}{10}\cdot (r) \\
&= \frac{1}{10}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $z = \dfrac {\sqrt {y+1}}{x+y}.$
:question/worked-solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression in the denominator is not equal to zero, and

- the expression under the square root is non-negative.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities:

$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}y + 1 \ge  0 \\ x + y \ne  0\end{array} \right. }
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}y \ge  - 1 \\ y \ne  - x\end{array} \right. }
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, y \geq -1, \: y \neq -x \big\}.
$$

{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}x + y > 0 \\ x + y \ne  1\end{array} \right. }

$$

$$

The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$\begin{cases}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{cases}\hspace{2em}⟹\hspace{2em}\begin{cases}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{cases}$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$\{(x,y)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.$$

:question/problem:
The function $f(x,y)$ is defined as 

$$
f(x,y)=3{y}^{3}-x+2.
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(5,-1).$
:question/worked-solution:
To evaluate our multivariable function at the point $(5,-1),$ we substitute $x=5$ and $y=-1$ into the function expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,-1) & =(3{y}^{3}-x+2){|}_{(5,-1)} \\  & =3(-1)^{3}-5+2 \\  & =-3-5+2 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

$$

:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$

:question/problem: Evaluate $z=\sqrt{x{y}^{2}-4}$ at the point $(5,-2).$

$$

$$

\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y\ne x+1\}.
$$

Points on either side of the line are allowed. Only the line $y=x+1$ is excluded.

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\dfrac{\sqrt{y+1}}{\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}-1}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Three conditions must hold:

- The numerator's radicand is nonnegative: $y+1\ge 0$.
- The denominator's radicand is nonnegative: $4-x^2-y^2\ge 0$.
- The whole denominator is nonzero: $\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}-1\ne 0$.

The first two conditions give $y\ge -1$ and $x^2+y^2\le 4$. To find the excluded points within this region, solve the denominator-zero equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}-1&=0\\
\sqrt{4-x^2-y^2}&=1\\
4-x^2-y^2&=1\\
x^2+y^2&=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring introduces no extra solutions here: both sides of the square-root equation are nonnegative. Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y\ge -1,\ x^2+y^2\le 4,\ x^2+y^2\ne 3\}.
$$

The outer boundary $x^2+y^2=4$ is allowed wherever $y\ge -1$: there the denominator is $-1$, not zero. The excluded circle has $x^2+y^2=3$, and only its portion in the allowed region matters. For example, $(2,0)$ and $(0,-1)$ are in the domain, while $(\sqrt{3},0)$ is excluded.

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\dfrac{\sqrt{y+2}}{x+y-1}$.
:question/worked-solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which both conditions hold:

- The expression under the square root is nonnegative.
- The denominator is nonzero.

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+2&\ge 0 &&\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\ge -2,\\
x+y-1&\ne 0 &&\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\ne 1-x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y\ge -2,\ y\ne 1-x\}.
$$

A zero numerator is allowed, so the boundary $y=-2$ is included except at $(3,-2)$, where the denominator is zero. The denominator may be positive or negative.

:question/problem:
The real-valued function $f(x,y)$ is defined by

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{\log_2(xy^2)+\sqrt{x-y}}{2^{-y}-x}.
$$

Evaluate this function at the point $(2,-2)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $x=2$ and $y=-2$ throughout the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(2,-2) &= \frac{\log_2\bigl(2(-2)^2\bigr)+\sqrt{2-(-2)}}{2^{-(-2)}-2} \\
        &= \frac{\log_2(8)+\sqrt{4}}{2^2-2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The logarithm has positive argument $8$, the square root has nonnegative argument $4$, and the denominator is $4-2=2$, which is nonzero. Thus the expression is defined over the real numbers. Since $2^3=8$, we have $\log_2(8)=3$, and the principal square root of $4$ is $2$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(2,-2) &= \frac{3+2}{4-2} \\
        &= \frac{5}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{2y-x}{x^3-y^2-7}
$$

at the point $(2,-1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $x=2$ and $y=-1$ into both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y-x &= 2(-1)-2 = -4, \\
x^3-y^2-7 &= 2^3-(-1)^2-7 \\
            &= 8-1-7 = 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

This would require division by zero, so $f(2,-1)$ is undefined. The point $(2,-1)$ is outside the domain; the nonzero numerator does not change that.

:question/problem: Evaluate $z=x^2+xy-5$ at the point $(-2,3)$.
:question/worked-solution:
The first coordinate gives $x=-2$ and the second gives $y=3$. Substitute both values, keeping parentheses around the negative input:

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= (-2)^2+(-2)(3)-5 \\
  &= 4-6-5 \\
  &= -7.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of the function at $(-2,3)$ is $-7$.

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{y}}{2y+x-4}$.
:question/worked-solution:
The numerator radicand must be nonnegative, and the polynomial denominator must be nonzero. A zero numerator is allowed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\ge0\\
2y+x-4&\ne 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2y+x\ne4
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y\ge0,\ 2y+x\ne4\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{y-x^2+1}}{\sqrt{1-\left(2x^3-y\right)}}$.
:question/worked-solution:
The numerator radicand may equal zero. The denominator radicand must be strictly positive, since its square root is the complete denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-x^2+1&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x^2\ge-1\\
1-\left(2x^3-y\right)&>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2x^3-y<1
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y-x^2\ge-1,\ 2x^3-y<1\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{-1-\left(y-x\right)}}{\sqrt{2y^3-x-1}}$.
:question/worked-solution:
The numerator radicand may equal zero. The denominator radicand must be strictly positive, since its square root is the complete denominator.

$$
\begin{aligned}
-1-\left(y-x\right)&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\le-1\\
2y^3-x-1&>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2y^3-x>1
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y-x\le-1,\ 2y^3-x>1\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{x+y}{\sqrt{2y+x-2}}$.
:question/worked-solution:
The numerator is a polynomial. The denominator radicand must be nonnegative and its square root must be nonzero, so the radicand must be strictly positive.

$$
\begin{aligned}
2y+x-2&>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2y+x>2
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,2y+x>2\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x-y^2+1}}{2y^3-x-1}$.

The numerator radicand must be nonnegative, and the polynomial denominator must be nonzero. A zero numerator is allowed.

$$
\begin{aligned}

2y^3-x-1&\ne 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2y^3-x\ne1
\end{aligned}
$$



Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,x-y^2\ge-1,\ 2y^3-x\ne1\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2-9}-2}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Both radicands must be nonnegative. The complete shifted denominator must also be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\ge0\\
x^2+y^2-9&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x^2+y^2\ge9\\
\sqrt{x^2+y^2-9}-2&=0\\
\sqrt{x^2+y^2-9}&=2\\
x^2+y^2-9&=4\\
x^2+y^2&=13
\end{aligned}
$$

The right side of the root equation is positive, so squaring is reversible. Exclude this level set. The radicand-zero boundary remains allowed wherever the numerator is real, since the denominator there is $-2$.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,\begin{aligned}y &\ge0\\x^2+y^2 &\ge9\\x^2+y^2 &\ne13\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{0-\left(y-x\right)}}{\sqrt{9-\left(y^2+x^2\right)}+1}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Both radicands must be nonnegative. The complete shifted denominator must also be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0-\left(y-x\right)&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\le0\\
9-\left(y^2+x^2\right)&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^2+x^2\le9\\
\sqrt{9-\left(y^2+x^2\right)}+1&\ge 1>0
\end{aligned}
$$

A principal square root is nonnegative. This denominator is always positive on the real-radicand region, so it has no zero to exclude. Squaring an equation with a negative right side would create extraneous points.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y-x\le0,\ y^2+x^2\le9\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{y^2+x^2-9}+2}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Both radicands must be nonnegative. The complete shifted denominator must also be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y\ge0\\
y^2+x^2-9&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^2+x^2\ge9\\
\sqrt{y^2+x^2-9}+2&\ge 2>0
\end{aligned}
$$

A principal square root is nonnegative. This denominator is always positive on the real-radicand region, so it has no zero to exclude. Squaring an equation with a negative right side would create extraneous points.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,y\ge0,\ y^2+x^2\ge9\}.
$$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{0-\left(y-x\right)}}{\sqrt{4-\left(y^2+x^2\right)}-1}$.
:question/worked-solution:
Both radicands must be nonnegative. The complete shifted denominator must also be nonzero.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0-\left(y-x\right)&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\le0\\
4-\left(y^2+x^2\right)&\ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^2+x^2\le4\\
\sqrt{4-\left(y^2+x^2\right)}-1&=0\\
\sqrt{4-\left(y^2+x^2\right)}&=1\\
4-\left(y^2+x^2\right)&=1\\
y^2+x^2&=3
\end{aligned}
$$

The right side of the root equation is positive, so squaring is reversible. Exclude this level set. The radicand-zero boundary remains allowed wherever the numerator is real, since the denominator there is $-1$.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\,:\,\begin{aligned}y-x &\le0\\y^2+x^2 &\le4\\y^2+x^2 &\ne3\end{aligned}\right\}.
$$

:question/problem: Which of the following shaded regions corresponds to the domain of the real-valued function $f(x,y)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{x - y - 1}}$?

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(x\right)}{y}.$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{y^{2}}{\ln\left(-2x^{2}+y-1\right)}.$

On positive inputs, $\ln\left(-2x^{2}+y-1\right)=0$ exactly when $-2x^{2}+y-1=1$. Thus we must exclude $-2x^{2}+y-1=1$, even when the numerator is zero.

Intersecting these conditions gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x^{2}+y-1>0 \\ -2x^{2}+y-1\ne 1\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(1-x^{2}\right)}{y+2}.$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(-x+2y-1\right)}{e^{x+2}}.$

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\ln\left(-x+2y-2\right)}{\sqrt{x+2}}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2y-2>0 \\ x+2>0\end{aligned}

:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $f(x,y)=\arcsin\left(x+\sqrt{y}\right).$

Therefore, the domain is

$$

$$

:question/problem:
Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=x\cdot \sin\left(y\right)
$$

at the point $(-2,\frac{\pi}{4})$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $x=-2$ and $y=\frac{\pi}{4}$ throughout the expression. Keep parentheses around signed inputs:

$$
f(-2,\frac{\pi}{4})=(-2)\cdot \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
$$

Evaluate the inner operations before combining them:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) &=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\
(-2)\cdot \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) &=- \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(-2,\frac{\pi}{4})=- \sqrt{2}$.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=\sqrt{x\cdot {y}^{2}+2}
$$

at the point $(-2,1)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $x=-2$ and $y=1$ throughout the expression. Keep parentheses around signed inputs:

$$
f(-2,1)=\sqrt{(-2)\cdot {1}^{2}+2}
$$

Evaluate the inner operations before combining them:

$$
\begin{aligned}
{1}^{2} &=1 \\
(-2)\cdot {1}^{2} &=-2 \\
(-2)\cdot {1}^{2}+2 &=0 \\
\sqrt{(-2)\cdot {1}^{2}+2} &=0
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(-2,1)=0$.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=2\cdot \arctan\left(y\right)-x
$$

at the point $(\pi,-1)$.

Substitute $x=\pi$ and $y=-1$ throughout the expression. Keep parentheses around signed inputs:

$$
f(\pi,-1)=2\cdot \arctan\left((-1)\right)-\pi
$$

Evaluate the inner operations before combining them:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\arctan\left((-1)\right) &=- \frac{\pi}{4} \\
2\cdot \arctan\left((-1)\right) &=- \frac{\pi}{2} \\
2\cdot \arctan\left((-1)\right)-\pi &=- \frac{3 \pi}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(\pi,-1)=- \frac{3 \pi}{2}$.

:question/problem:
Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}}{\arcsin\left(x\right)}
$$

at the point $(1,2)$.

Evaluate the real-valued function

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{\log_{3}\left({x}^{2}+y-6\right)}{\sqrt{x-y+10}}
$$

at the point $(2,3)$.
:question/worked-solution:
Substitute $x=2$ and $y=3$ throughout the expression. Keep parentheses around signed inputs:

$$
f(2,3)=\frac{\log_{3}\left({2}^{2}+3-6\right)}{\sqrt{2-3+10}}
$$

Evaluate the inner operations before combining them:

$$
\begin{aligned}
{2}^{2} &=4 \\
{2}^{2}+3 &=7 \\
{2}^{2}+3-6 &=1 \\

:question/problem:

$$

at the point $(1,-2)$.

Substitute $x=1$ and $y=-2$ throughout the expression. Keep parentheses around signed inputs:

$$

Evaluate the inner operations before combining them:

$$
\begin{aligned}

\log_{2}\left(1\cdot {(-2)}^{2}\right) &=2 \\

\sqrt{1-(-2)+6} &=3 \\

(-1)\cdot (-2) &=2 \\

:question/problem:
Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0), (1,0)$ and $(0,2),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\cos{y}\,\mathrm{d}x+x\sin{y}\,\mathrm{d}y}= \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \,\textrm d A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise. Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/a7/a78a98750e3203760d27daaebd42852198538935e2c3777a0b8a8c85d1bb0901.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= \cos{y}$ and $Q(x,y)= x\sin{y}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y) = 2\sin{y}.$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](images/a8/a87f696b1eb42588ab69800b72d821bf47b35676fc19dcd4fe2927bbf36ba3f8.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= 4x^2y$ and $Q(x,y)= 2y^2.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 1,\, 2x \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}4{x}^{2}y\,dx+2{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}(-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(2-2x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & =-8{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{1}{12} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r,
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle xy+y^2,\,2x^2+e^y\rangle$ and $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=x^2$ and $y=2x$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/5f/5f34ac74599937e0ae181126ff9a3da5b29dfe213614a1f23ca10c7062f22f7d.png)

Writing the vector line integral in differential form gives

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\oint_C(xy+y^2)\,dx+(2x^2+e^y)\,dy.
$$

Here $P=xy+y^2$ and $Q=2x^2+e^y$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=x+2y,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=4x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=3x-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersections satisfy $x^2=2x$, so $x(x-2)=0$ and $x=0,2$. On $0\le x\le2$, the parabola $y=x^2$ is below the line $y=2x$. Thus $D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le2x\}$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
&=\int_0^2\int_{x^2}^{2x}(3x-2y)\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2[3xy-y^2]_{x^2}^{2x}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2\bigl((6x^2-4x^2)-(3x^3-x^4)\bigr)\,dx\\
&=\int_0^2(x^4-3x^3+2x^2)\,dx\\
&=\left[\frac{x^5}{5}-\frac{3x^4}{4}+\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^2\\
&=\frac{32}{5}-12+\frac{16}{3}=-\frac{4}{15}.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate

$$
\oint_C xy\,dx+(x^2+y^2)\,dy,
$$

where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,2)$ and $(0,2)$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/a8/a87f696b1eb42588ab69800b72d821bf47b35676fc19dcd4fe2927bbf36ba3f8.png)

Here $P=xy$ and $Q=x^2+y^2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=x,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2x,\\
Q_x-P_y&=x.\end{aligned}
$$

The sloping side through $(0,0)$ and $(1,2)$ is $y=2x$. Vertical slices run from $y=2x$ to $y=2$, with $0\le x\le1$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C xy\,dx+(x^2+y^2)\,dy
&=\int_0^1\int_{2x}^{2}x\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1[xy]_{2x}^{2}\,dx\\
&=\int_0^1(2x-2x^2)\,dx\\
&=\left[x^2-\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\\
&=1-\frac23=\frac13.
\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem:

$$

where $C$ is the boundary of the rectangle $-1\le x\le3$, $0\le y\le2$, traversed counterclockwise.
:question/worked-solution:
The curve $C$ is a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve. The component functions have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, so Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,dA.
$$

The enclosed region $D$ and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/39/3954846460076fa1ef1e5826d32bde9145e7350cb2324072b001d8c6ff41cc14.png)

Here $P=2y-x$ and $Q=5x+y$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=2,\qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=5,\\
Q_x-P_y&=3.\end{aligned}
$$

The bounds of $D$ are $-1\le x\le3$ and $0\le y\le2$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C (2y-x)\,dx+(5x+y)\,dy
&=\int_{-1}^{3}\int_0^2 3\,dy\,dx\\
&=\int_{-1}^{3}[3y]_0^2\,dx\\
&=\int_{-1}^{3}6\,dx\\
&=[6x]_{-1}^{3}\\
&=18-(-6)\\
&=24.
\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, the constant curl $3$ is multiplied by the rectangle's area $(3-(-1))(2-0)=8$.

:question/problem:
The curve $C$ follows the straight sides of a square in the order

$$
(0,0)\longrightarrow(0,1)\longrightarrow(1,1)\longrightarrow(1,0)\longrightarrow(0,0).
$$

Let $D$ be the interior of the square. Which function $f(x,y)$ is obtained by applying Green's theorem with this traversal in

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\oint_C\left(ye^{xy}+y^2\right)\,\mathrm{d}x
+\left(xe^{xy}+x^2y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\\
&\qquad=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The ordered vertices trace the left side upward, the top side to the right, the right side downward and the bottom side to the left. The interior stays on the traveler's right, so $C$ is clockwise.

![The shaded unit square with arrows pointing clockwise.](images/91/91aadfb7b45c720c35a0aca6158d87f5e5eae700f9537f259015236df3359c7e.png)

Reversing a curve reverses the sign of its line integral. Thus the clockwise version of Green's theorem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
&=-\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A\\
&=\iint_D(P_y-Q_x)\,\mathrm{d}A.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $P=ye^{xy}+y^2$ and $Q=xe^{xy}+x^2y$. Both functions have continuous first partial derivatives throughout the plane. Apply the product and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2y,\\
Q_x&=e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now use the order of subtraction appropriate to this clockwise traversal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=P_y-Q_x\\
&=\left(e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2y\right)
-\left(e^{xy}+xy e^{xy}+2xy\right)\\
&=2y-2xy\\
&=2y(1-x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Both exponential terms cancel. Using $Q_x-P_y$ without correcting the orientation would instead give $2xy-2y$, the negative of the required integrand.

:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$ and $(0,1)$, traversed counterclockwise, and let $D$ be its interior. Use Green's theorem to choose the integrand $f(x,y)$ in

$$
\oint_C y^2e^{xy}\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(2xy e^{xy}+x^2y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$, Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A,
$$

provided $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$.

The rectangle and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/8d/8d57fb7f6b8e2e822a11f11a0267994c449c37b43df167a8d48ab8036854b8dd.png)

Identify $P=y^2e^{xy}$ and $Q=2xy e^{xy}+x^2y$. Both required partial derivatives involve a product rule. The chain rule gives $\partial_y e^{xy}=xe^{xy}$ and $\partial_x e^{xy}=ye^{xy}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=2y e^{xy}+xy^2e^{xy},\\
Q_x&=2y e^{xy}+2xy^2e^{xy}+2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract the entire derivative $P_y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=Q_x-P_y\\
&=\left(2y e^{xy}+2xy^2e^{xy}+2xy\right)
-\left(2y e^{xy}+xy^2e^{xy}\right)\\
&=xy^2e^{xy}+2xy.
\end{aligned}
$$

The $2y e^{xy}$ terms cancel, but only one of the two $xy^2e^{xy}$ terms cancels. Hence the line integral equals $\iint_D\left(xy^2e^{xy}+2xy\right)\,\mathrm{d}A$.

:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$, traversed counterclockwise, and let $D$ be its interior. According to Green's theorem,

$$
\oint_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}x+(xy+x^2)\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

Which function $f(x,y)$ is obtained by applying Green's theorem?
:question/worked-solution:
For a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$, Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y
=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A,
$$

provided $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$.

The region and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/aa/aa60dd35a920d166f7cc3238a366bde93bd2c33e1b39b0a38313ab46a8de2d8b.png)

Here $P(x,y)=y^2$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+x^2$. Holding $x$ constant in $P_y$ and $y$ constant in $Q_x$, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}&=2y,\\
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}&=y+2x.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x,y)&=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\\
&=(y+2x)-2y\\
&=2x-y.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the line integral equals $\iint_D(2x-y)\,\mathrm{d}A$. The task stops at the integrand; no integration is needed.

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_y&=3,\\
Q_x&=-1,\\
Q_x-P_y&=-4.
\end{aligned}

:question/problem:
The curves $y=x^2$ and $y=x+2$ enclose a region $D$. Its boundary $C$ is traversed counterclockwise. For

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle \ln(x+2)-y^2,\,x^2+xy+y^2\rangle,
$$

use Green's theorem to express $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r$ as a repeated integral, integrating with respect to $y$ first. Do not evaluate the integral.
:question/worked-solution:
For a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$, Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

The component functions here have continuous first partial derivatives on an open set containing $D$. Writing $\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r=P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y$, we have $P=\ln(x+2)-y^2$ and $Q=x^2+xy+y^2$. Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}P_y&=-2y,\\Q_x&=2x+y,\\Q_x-P_y&=(2x+y)-(-2y)\\&=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

The logarithm contributes nothing to $P_y$ because it depends only on $x$.

To find the outer limits, solve for the intersections:

$$
\begin{aligned}x^2&=x+2,\\(x-2)(x+1)&=0,\\x&=-1\ \text{or}\ x=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Between these values,

$$
(x+2)-x^2=(2-x)(x+1)\ge0,
$$

so the parabola is the lower boundary and the line is the upper boundary. The region is shown below.

![](images/e3/e32b8e7d6ce80d7cedad928f9a2f7acc3c3d7f06add7909e856db27d154068d6.png)

Thus

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le x+2\}.
$$

Since $x+2\ge1$ on $D$, the logarithm and both component functions are smooth on an open neighborhood of this region. Applying Green's theorem yields

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r=\int_{-1}^{2}\int_{x^2}^{x+2}\left(2x+3y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Using $0$ as the outer lower limit would omit the part of the region to the left of the $y$-axis. Subtracting $2y$ instead of subtracting $-2y$ would give the wrong curl.

:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the rectangle $D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le3\}$, traversed counterclockwise. Use Green's theorem in the form

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

Which repeated integral, integrating with respect to $y$ first, represents the following line integral? Do not evaluate it.

$$
\oint_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}x+xy\,\mathrm{d}y
$$
:question/worked-solution:
For a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$, Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

The component functions here have continuous first partial derivatives on an open set containing $D$. Here $P=y^2$ and $Q=xy$, so

$$
P_y=2y,\qquad Q_x=y,\qquad Q_x-P_y=y-2y=-y.
$$

The rectangle is shown below.

![](images/6f/6f831b2b707e63e8eb34ff5f6c1c45d0267f51001de2560834d212506b48ee41.png)

For each fixed $x$, the inner variable $y$ runs from $0$ to $3$; the outer variable $x$ runs from $-1$ to $2$. Thus

$$
\oint_C y^2\,\mathrm{d}x+xy\,\mathrm{d}y=\int_{-1}^{2}\int_{0}^{3}\left(-y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x.
$$

Adding the two partial derivatives would give $3y$; Green's theorem requires their difference. The bounds must stay attached to their corresponding variables.

:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(0,-1)$ and $(1,0)$, traversed counterclockwise. For

$$
\mathbf F(x,y)=\langle y^2+x^2,\,xy+x^2\rangle,
$$

use Green's theorem to express $\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r$ as a repeated integral, integrating with respect to $x$ first. Do not evaluate the integral.
:question/worked-solution:
For a counterclockwise, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve $C$ bounding $D$, Green's theorem gives

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

The component functions here have continuous first partial derivatives on an open set containing $D$. The vector notation means

$$
\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r=(y^2+x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x+(xy+x^2)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$

Thus $P=y^2+x^2$ and $Q=xy+x^2$, giving

$$
P_y=2y,\qquad Q_x=y+2x,\qquad Q_x-P_y=2x-y.
$$

The triangle and its counterclockwise boundary are shown below.

![](images/6d/6d4f13abad5cc193dccedee3114fbd9cbd9fb8e6b5b3ddb0d07f0ed2ed51f4ff.png)

The sloping edge joins $(0,-1)$ to $(1,0)$, so its equation is $x=y+1$. At each height $-1\le y\le0$, a horizontal slice starts at $x=0$ and ends at $x=y+1$. Therefore

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le y\le0,\ 0\le x\le y+1\},
$$

and

$$
\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf r=\int_{-1}^{0}\int_{0}^{y+1}\left(2x-y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$

The inner bounds depend on the outer variable $y$. Reversing the curl difference would reverse the sign even though the curve remains counterclockwise.

:question/problem:
Let $C$ be the boundary of the unit square, traversed counterclockwise, and let $D$ be its interior.

Use Green's theorem to choose the function $f(x,y)$ in

$$
\begin{aligned}&\oint_C\left(- x^{2} y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&\quad+\left(x^{3} y - 2 \sin{\left(y \right)}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$
:question/worked-solution:
The stated traversal is **counterclockwise**. Green's theorem applies because both coefficients have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$. For this orientation,

$$
\oint_C P\,\mathrm{d}x+Q\,\mathrm{d}y=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathrm{d}A.
$$

![The region and oriented boundary.](images/aa/aa60dd35a920d166f7cc3238a366bde93bd2c33e1b39b0a38313ab46a8de2d8b.png)

Identify the coefficients of the two differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y)&=- x^{2} y^{2},\\Q(x,y)&=x^{3} y - 2 \sin{\left(y \right)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hold the other variable constant when taking each partial derivative. Apply the power rule to each relevant term.

$$
\begin{aligned}P_y&=- 2 x^{2} y,\\Q_x&=3 x^{2} y.\end{aligned}
$$

Subtract the entire derivative in the order required by the traversal, then collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)&=Q_x-P_y\\&=\left(3 x^{2} y\right)\\&\quad-\left(- 2 x^{2} y\right)\\&=5 x^{2} y.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $f(x,y)=5 x^{2} y$. No evaluation of the double integral is needed.

$$

$$

Hold the other variable constant when taking each partial derivative. Apply the product and chain rules where required.

$$
\begin{aligned}P_y&=x y^{2} e^{x y} + 2 y e^{x y},\\Q_x&=- x y^{2} e^{x y} + 2 x y - y e^{x y}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}

$$

$$
